#3571. Where Is Beth Holloway Today? Natalee Holloway’s Mom Is Still Seeking Justice

Beth Holloway’s life turned upside down in 2005 when her daughter, Natalee Holloway, went missing during a high school graduation trip in Aruba. While Joran van der Sloot admitted to killing the teen in 2023, Beth is still fighting for justice because he has not been charged for the murder.

After Beth appeared in Netflix’s November 2026 docuseries Natalee Holloway: Taken, viewers have been left wondering what else she is up to today and where Natlee’s murder case stands now.

Beth was working as a public school speech pathologist at the time Natalee went missing. She stepped away from the role for nearly 10 years while she was searching for her daughter.

More than two decades later, Beth revealed that she’s back in the classroom. “I think it’s good for the body to stay in motion and keep busy,” she said, according to Netflix’s Tudum. “And no idle time here, none.”

Beth also shared that she works with families of other missing people.

“Since so many people had reached out to help me, being a teacher, I found myself wanting to give back and share what I’ve learned with others since they had given so much to me,” she explained. “Sometimes I’m just there to facilitate communication with law enforcement. Maybe they need help facilitating search and rescue resources, personnel, guidance.”

Natalee was 18 years old when she went missing while on a vacation to Oranjestad, Aruba. She was last seen on May 30, 2005, while leaving a nightclub and getting into a car with van der Sloot, Deepak Kalpoe and Satish Kalpoe.

The three men quickly became suspects in the case and were arrested twice throughout the investigation. They were released both times after authorities failed to find enough evidence to charge them with Natalee’s murder.

In 2010, van der Sloot was arrested for the murder of 21-year-old college student Stephany Flores Ramírez in Peru. That same year, he was indicted in the United States on federal wire fraud and extortion charges tied to a meeting he and Beth had in March 2010, in which he demanded money in exchange for information about Natalee’s disappearance.

Van der Sloot ultimately pleaded guilty to the federal extortion charges in 2023, and he was sentenced to 20 years in prison. The sentence is currently running concurrently with his 28-year sentence for Ramírez’s murder.

As part of his plea deal, van der Sloot admitted that he killed Natalee and agreed to share information about her death.

Despite admitting to her murder, van der Sloot was never prosecuted for Natalee’s murder because Aruba enforces a 12-year statute of limitations for homicides. The window to convict him had closed since the time he confessed.

Beth reflected on van der Sloot’s confession in Natalee Holloway: Taken, as well as while talking to Tudum.

“The nightmare’s over, right? But I’m not done yet,” she said.

Beth explained that she has spent the last two years working behind the scenes with Netherlands-based attorneys Royce de Vries and Annemiek van Spanje to file a murder complaint against van der Sloot with Dutch authorities.

“I’ve been working busy behind the scenes, got the murder complaint,” Beth said. “And now we’re working on, hopefully, murder charges. So I’ve been busy, but one step at a time.”

The Hunger Games movies became a sensation upon their release, with the public obsessed with the book-to-screen adaptations. Luckily for fans, we're returned to Panem thanks to Suzanne Collins' prequels. We're very close to the release of Francis Lawrence's Sunrise on the Reaping, which tells the story of Haymitch's Games. But should moviegoers read the novel before heading to theaters? I asked that very question to both the director and star, Joseph Zada.

What we know about Sunrise on the Reaping depends on if you read the source material, but fans are preparing for a heartbreaking story about the second Quarter Quell. I had the privilege of speaking with Zada about the blockbuster and asked him if fans should read the book or go in blind. He told me:

I think, I think actually maybe if you have read the book, because you know it's coming the whole time. That's always such a horrible feeling when you know what's coming. I brought that into the last bit of the film. It's like my character in the back of his head knows what's, what's coming. Horrible. Horrible. But I also think, yeah, it would be a bit shocking having no idea coming back. Either or. Each their own. You don't have to be a fan either to watch this.

There's no correct way to watch the new Hunger Games flick, but those who read Sunrise on the Reaping know exactly what tragedies are coming. That's how I watched the film, and as soon as certain doomed characters appeared, my stomach dropped, knowing when they would die and how. You can see my conversation with the East of Eden star below:

A post shared by CinemaBlend (@cinemablend)

Of course, I had to ask the movie's director this same question. Francis Lawrence has a long history with the franchise, having directed five out of the six Hunger Games movies. He weighed in on whether he thinks one should go into Sunrise on the Reaping with or without knowledge of what happened in its corresponding novel. He told me:

What I like about this story is that I think, quite honestly, you could come, this could be your entry point into the series. And I think you could come in fresh, don't know anything about the movies, go and see this thing. You start, you get behind this kid that you love, and you go on this ride, and you start to meet these characters, and then you could go out from there. 'Cause I think a lot of the times people think, 'Oh, you have to have this to then be able to sort of look at and understand who the young people are.' But I think you can go the other way too. But I think you can, you could go into this fresh not knowing anything. And not even having read the book, and I think you'll have a very emotional experience.

He's not wrong. While there will be fans who have read and watched every single Hunger Games story, newbies can also walk in fresh to Sunrise on the Reaping. Any essential exposition is dropped to help those moviegoers, while the hardcore fandom will watch the prequel with the knowledge of what came before and after Haymitch's games.

Of course, there are plenty of moments in this new movie that longtime fans will especially appreciate. Namely the spot-on impressions of Woody Harrelson and Jeffrey Wright that are being performed by Joseph Zada and Kelvin Harrison Jr. respectively. Conversely, folks who read the book are burdened with knowing what happens to the characters in the new Hunger Games movie, while casual fans will be able to be shocked by all of the new movie's twists.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will hit theaters on November 20th as part of the 2026 movie release list. Meanwhile, fans can rewatch all of the previous movies with their Hulu subscription.

#3568. Dua Lipa Talks About Her Book Club, and Her Favorite Authors Join Her for a Photo

It’s the 41st week of this year, and Dua Lipa has already read 22 books. Next up is Sufiyaan Salam’s novel, Wimmy Road Boyz, a coming of age story about a British Pakistani friend group. But fresh on her mind is Careless People: A Cautionary Tale of Power, Greed, and Lost Idealism by Sarah Wynn-Williams, which Lipa has just finished, logging the accomplishment in the Notes app on her orange iPhone.

“Do you know about it?” she asks me, eager to recommend the whistleblower’s memoir. “She’s getting censored because she started working at Facebook very early on and she dishes it all out.”

PAGE TURNERS Lipa at Albertine Books in October with seven of her hand-selected Service95 book club monthly reads. Shirt by Gucci; jewelry by Bulgari.

It should come as no surprise that Lipa, the internet’s favorite hardworking “vacanza queen,” gets most of her reading done while traveling. “I can read in cars. I don’t get sick. It’s kind of a flex,” she says. When we meet in New York in early October, Lipa has just returned from a trip to Madrid, where she performed with Shakira, doing what she humbly refers to as her “day job,” and Paris, for a Chanel show. No matter the destination, for work or play, Lipa will always toss a book—no e-readers—in her bag. “I love the feeling of a book. I love when all the pages get all fucked up a little bit,” she says.

Dressed in an off-duty uniform of blue jeans, a black Chanel sweater, leather boots, and a black Gucci purse big enough to stash a hardcover or two, Lipa, the 31-year-old British Albanian singer who has emerged as a leading literacy advocate, is gearing up for the London Literature Festival, which she guest-curated this year.

Her reading habit is impressive. Not just because she is a jet-set Grammy Award–winning pop star and half of a newlywed power couple (she and husband Callum Turner famously bonded over finishing the same chapter of Hernan Diaz’s novel, Trust) whose Instagram suggests that she exists in a perpetual state of glamour, but because, according to a recent statistic, more than half of American adults read approximately zero books in a year. “Sad,” Lipa says when I give her this stat.

Since 2021, Lipa has been using her spare time to run Service95—a website, newsletter, book club, and podcast—described as a “cultural concierge.” Through the platform, Lipa offers bespoke recommendations and publishes writing on a wide range of topics from style, travel, and wellness to politics and activism. It’s also where, since Service95’s inception, she has hosted in-depth conversations with authors from around the world and across genres. With dozens of podcast episodes under her belt so far, she’s quickly learned what it’s like to be on the other side of an interview. “I’ve done so many interviews myself and I’ve had to answer the same question over and over again. I’m quite sensitive to the fact that I don’t want to put the author in the same position of having to repeat themselves,” she says. “It’s one of my favorite things that I do. I feel like I get so much out of the conversations.”

Today, at the Villa Albertine, a French cultural institution on the Upper East Side, she’s brought her bookshelf to life, gathering seven of her favorite writers—memoirists, novelists, journalists, a National Book Award and Booker Prize winner—for a class photo. Standing together in one room, beneath a mural of a constellation, the stars align: Douglas Stuart, Brit Bennett, Patti Smith, Roxane Gay, Jennifer Clement, Patrick Radden Keefe, Min Jin Lee, and Lipa, all looking like the English department of your wildest dreams. Sitting next to Smith, the author of Just Kids, Lipa, one of the biggest celebrities in the world, appears to be starstruck. In a rare role reversal, Lipa is the fangirl, whipping out her phone to commemorate the occasion with a group selfie.

Here, her impact in the literary world is undeniable—and so is her range.

Between takes, Smith inquires about how many languages Lipa speaks—English, Albanian, some Spanish, and she’s learning French and Italian, she says. The Just Kids author quips that she only knows how to ask where the “biblioteca” is. “That’s kind of all you need,” jokes Keefe, author of Say Nothing, who tells me he often encounters young readers who were introduced to his work via Service95.

READ THE ROOM Dua Lipa and authors take a selfie at Albertine Books. Lipa’s shoes by Prada; jewelry by Bulgari.

Watching all of these literary titans in conversation with each other, it’s impressive to see them all embrace Lipa as an advocate of their work. “I’m sure that there are lots of other things she could be doing with her time that would be far more profitable than championing books,” says Bennett, author of The Vanishing Half. “It’s amazing that she does this out of a genuine love for reading.”

“It’s fun work. It’s good work,” insists Lipa, who is happy to disprove naysayers who think she just “holidays all the time.” “I’m having a good time, and I get all my work done, and I do what I want to do, and then I go on holiday, and I’m happy with that.” It’s what keeps her motivated: “Sometimes being underestimated gives me extra fire in my belly.”

In 2023, when Lipa launched her book club, which has racked up nearly 1 million Instagram followers, she joined the likes of Oprah Winfrey, Reese Witherspoon, Kaia Gerber, Dakota Johnson, Emma Roberts, and Jenna Bush Hager. But the saturation of the celebrity book club market gave her no hesitation. “If people feel a little bit inclined to just go and pick up a book and read something, we’re all doing our job,” she says. “I don’t care if someone’s going to go to this book club or the next one. As long as they’re reading, I’m happy.”

But Clement, author of Widow Basquiat, considers Service95 to be in a league of its own. “It is not simply curating individual titles; it is curating perspective,” she says. “Almost as if, taken together, the books themselves are forming an arc, a larger story unfolding through the choices.”

Lipa works closely with her book club director, Maria Padget, but selects Service95's monthly reads herself, guided not by what’s trending but instead, as Lee, the author of Pachinko who calls Lipa an “exemplary literary citizen,” puts it, by honoring “her intellectual curiosity,” often highlighting marginalized voices, and not absorbing literature through a strictly Western lens.

“When she looks at her readers, she doesn’t think what would be easiest for you to enjoy, or what would comfort you or challenge you the least,” says Stuart, author of Shuggie Bain. “Instead she signals, go on, you can read this, you should read this; read this challenging book, read this banned book, and see what they want to deny you, see what you can achieve and have access to what would make you more powerful!”

In the face of a burgeoning literacy crisis, global book bans, rampant censorship, and the rise of artificial intelligence, Service95 is a venue for Lipa to educate herself and her readers on global issues—encouraging an open dialogue and discourse. “I don’t shy away from it. I also like the fact that I do it on my own terms,” says Lipa, who calls activism an “important pillar” of Service95.

As a result, she’s spoken to Margaret Atwood about the fight for female reproductive rights and discussed sexual violence and intersectional feminism with Gay, author of Bad Feminist. “The book had already been out for more than a decade, so it was quite a thrill to see her introducing the work to a new audience,” the essayist says. Lipa has also pondered the impacts of AI with Nobel Prize laureate Kazuo Ishiguro and provided required reading on Israel and the war in Gaza. She’s even joined a reading group at a women’s prison in Surrey and opened the Manifesto Library—stocking banned books inside the Livraria Lello in Portugal.

“The whole goal was to get people to take a breather, learn about the thing that’s happening, and not to be afraid to ask questions or not be right all the time,” she says.

Lipa, who admits to using the Opal app, which limits her to an hour a day on social media to post her famous photo dumps, is hopeful Service95 can also serve as an antidote to doomscrolling and AI. “Not only are we declining in reading and not picking up a book, but the fact that you can have these cheat codes that completely bypass the whole point of the learning or the ingesting of information,” she says. “It’s just going to make us stupider as people.”

She credits her mother, Anesa, for her love of reading, reminiscing on their weekends spent at a London bookshop. “I basically would just sit there and read for hours and hours and hours. I loved it,” she says, rattling off the names of authors from her childhood, like Jacqueline Wilson and Malorie Blackman and the Mr. Men and Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen series. Reading is formative to who she is as an artist; it makes her a better songwriter, as she tells me, but it is also fundamental to who she is as a person. “I feel like we get a better understanding of ourselves, of our friends, of our family members, of the people around us, what they might be going through, what’s happening in their life by just picking up a book,” says Lipa.

When I bring up the recent claim from influencer Alix Earle that she had never read a book (apart from maybe Dr. Seuss), Lipa considers the topic thoughtfully and speaks without passing any judgment, generously suggesting the possibility that maybe, as a public figure, Earle said this as a protective measure, to shield her from further prodding and criticism. “Books are so personal, I think people also get intimidated,” she says. “Books should just be enjoyable. No one’s expecting anything from the person reading it. You don’t have to overanalyze it. It’s just supposed to make you feel something.”

And true to form, she offers a book recommendation: “I love The Girls by Emma Cline. I think that’s a cool gateway drug book.”

For Lipa, it all harkens back to searching for that feeling. She returns to her recent interview with Ishiguro, the Klara and the Sun author, who drew parallels between pop music and literature and their ability to foster connection. “He said the heart has so many rooms, so many things that make us, and AI can’t do that,” she says. “There is something really encouraging about that, that some things can't be replicated. Our real humanness and the love we feel, the loneliness even, it can make us feel even more alive and more human.” Perhaps Lipa’s book club is an act of resistance, but it’s also, to borrow a line from her last album, an act of radical optimism.

#3567. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3566. Russell Brand Accused of Sexual Misconduct by 6 More Women After Sentencing

Russell Brand has been accused of sexual misconduct by six additional women in light of his rape conviction.

A Thursday, November 12, report by the Times of London claims that Brand, 51, had nonconsensual sex with multiple women. He is also accused of attempting to coerce a separate victim into a bathroom by arguing their interaction was consensual.

Per The Times, Brand’s new accusers had been attendees at his comedy shows who subsequently felt afraid to contact the police. They reportedly decided to come forward now in solidarity with the women who testified during his trial.

Brand, who has long maintained his innocence and entered a not guilty plea, was found guilty of three counts of sexual assault and one count of rape earlier this month. He was sentenced to 10 years in prison.

“I’m good, I’m good,” Brand mouthed to his legal team in the courtroom after the verdict was rendered.

The disgraced comedian had been accused of sexual assault, rape and emotional abuse by multiple women between 1999 to 2013. He long refuted the accusations.

“I’ve received two extremely disturbing letters, or a letter and an email, one from a mainstream media TV company [and] one from a newspaper, listing a litany of extremely egregious and aggressive attacks,” Brand said in a September 2023 social media video. “As well as some pretty stupid stuff, like my community festival should be stopped, that I shouldn’t be able to attack mainstream media narratives on this channel, but amidst this litany of astonishing, rather baroque attacks, are some very serious allegations that I absolutely refute.”

He continued at the time, “As I’ve written about extensively in my books, I was very, very promiscuous. Now during that time of promiscuity, the relationships I had were absolutely, always consensual. I was always transparent about that then — almost too transparent. And I’m being transparent about it now as well. And to see that transparency metastasized into something criminal that I absolutely deny makes me question [if] there is another agenda at play?”

Brand vehemently denied the “very, very, serious criminal allegations.”

Amid the scandal, Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, has stood by his side. (Brand and Gallacher, who got married in 2017, share three children.)

Gallacher, 39, testified in the proceedings, calling Brand a “wonderful father” and an “amazingly attentive husband.”

“The way he treats me is to really know me,” she said. “I feel very seen by him, in a way I’ve never experienced before. I love him very much.”

Their marriage even played a factor into the judge’s verdict of the actor’s sentence.

“Given how long ago these offenses were committed and the evidence of your wife, I accept there is no sound evidential basis for me to conclude you pose a risk for the future,” the judge said on Monday, November 9, per court docs obtained by Us.

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, contact the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-HOPE (4673).

#3565. In 'The Spot', Claire Danes and Ewan McGregor Unravel Together

Claire Danes was standing in the operating room, dressed in scrubs and a mask, when a surgeon’s assistant gave her the opposite of a pep talk. “You may think you’re badass, but if you think you’re fainting, you’re fainting, and we can’t have that, so just let me know,” she told Danes.

Danes, luckily, did not faint, though she says she was incredibly aware of her breathing as she watched an intricate brain surgery performed by a team of doctors.

The three-time Emmy winner was observing in preparation for her role in The Spot, a new Hulu series in which she plays a successful neurosurgeon who begins to suspect that she may be responsible for the hit-and-run death of a child. As she tries to investigate the horrific possibility, she and her husband (Ewan McGregor) find themselves falling deeper and deeper into a web of suspicion and dark secrets.

“I’ve always thought of it as an exploration of a marriage through the lens of a crime and maybe exploration of a crime through the lens of a marriage,” says Solomon of The Spot.

“I’m fascinated with this notion of what if your worst-case scenario way in the back of your head started to really look like it was true, and how could you dramatize that?” says writer, creator, and showrunner Ed Solomon.

The bold psychological thriller, which Vanity Fair can exclusively reveal will debut on January 13, follows a woman unraveling at the possibility of her worst fears coming true, and a marriage under enormous strain. There’s been a steady stream of whodunit miniseries in the last decade, but here Solomon, whose past work includes writing The Christophers and Now You See Me, has created a highly watchable, page-turning series that’s more of a “did I do it?”

“I never want it to be pretentious,” says Solomon. “I just want it to be fun and entertaining, but also elevated, respectful of the viewer.”

"I had wanted to work with Claire for years and we just had great fun acting and playing together while making this show,” says McGregor.

Danes was initially drawn to the series because of the portrait of the marriage at the heart of it, and Solomon’s particular gift for weaving the tragic into the comic. “It gets really very dark pretty quickly,” she says, “but it’s absurd too.”

She not only watched two brain surgeries in preparation but also shadowed a surgeon on his rounds, being with patients before they went into surgery and while they were recovering with their families. “I felt horrible that there I was in this room with these people who couldn’t be more vulnerable, and there I was, trying to be discreet in the corner,” she says.

But the experience gave her insight into what kind of person her character Lou Shadwick would be: intense, hypervigilant, and high achieving. “There’s a lot of marathon runners in there, and highly, highly focused people,” she says. “And they carry a lot of responsibility, and I think they compartmentalize very effectively.”

Danes had previously worked with Solomon on the 2023 series Full Circle, which was directed by Steven Soderbergh. When Kate Winslet, who was initially attached to play Lou, exited, Danes stepped in. Solomon needed an actress who could portray a mother and surgeon who is obsessed with doing the right thing and being a good person. “To be able to see someone who has a very, very present and active inner life that when you look, you can see well beyond the eyes and you can see someone who can be basically playing many things at one time, which was really important and interesting to me,” he says.

Danes had never worked with McGregor before, though they both had previously worked with Baz Luhrmann (on Romeo + Juliet and Moulin Rouge, respectively) and she thinks they had met briefly around that time. “We were definitely of a certain time, the ’90s,” she says. “So we share a lot of references, but it was just an immediate rapport.”

Lou is doing what many mothers juggling work and family have done: driving home from work, talking on the phone about dinner while also checking an unending flurry of text messages. It’s at that moment when she thinks she might have accidentally hit a child on a bike and not realized it until she heard about it later. “It’s so effective, this circumstance that he’s drawn for us,” she says of Solomon. “It’s entirely relatable, and I think it’s the fear that we all have experienced and hosted many, many times, if not on a daily basis.”

Michael Patrick Thornton as Pete Porphyry

As she tries to piece together what might have happened, a police officer (Daveed Diggs) and a detective (Michael Patrick Thornton) are doing the same, and begin to suspect Lou. Her husband, Damon, gets involved, making more trouble for both of them.

Lou and Damon met in medical school, but Damon dropped out and is now pursuing medical aid work in the shadow of his wife’s illustrious career. “I really like the idea of a man, who is charming and good-looking and therefore used to feeling very much in control when he walks into a room, having a spouse who is quite significantly on the rise,” says Solomon. “What does that do to your sense of ego if you’re a guy like that?”

Lou begins to see signs that she may be the guilty party.

McGregor says he had wanted to work with Danes for a long time, and was drawn as Damon as a character. “I think the character has an amazing arc throughout the story from where he starts to where he ends,” he says. “He has a very deeply hidden, shameful secret that gets uncovered as the story goes on.”

McGregor brings to the role a kind of playfulness. “I’ve always loved a certain quality of Ewan’s where there’s a maturity and a boyishness happening simultaneously,” says Solomon. “The boyish quality within this character is really important and the ability to cover a sense of wound.”

Set in upstate New York, the new series will take viewers on a wild ride following two people who are putting themselves in an increasingly dire situation and web of lies. “She’s a decent person, and so is her husband, really,” says Danes. “And yet, they allow their moral compass to become increasingly compromised.” Solomon hopes that even as the story gets darker and wilder, it will leave viewers with at least one big question they’ll have to grapple with: “I would hope that they’re asking questions, like what would I do if I were in that situation?”

“In Ewan, you can see the fragility in him,” says Solomon of McGregor.

#3563. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3's Two Big Character Deaths Explained

The land of Mordor is where the shadows lie, and this article is where major spoilers lie. Read no further if you haven't watched the Season 3 premiere episodes of "The Rings of Power."

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" has one thing in common with the TV phenomenon that was "Game of Thrones" — they're both exercises in enduring misery. After all, the show is all about watching stupid sexy Sauron (Charlie Vickers) make everyone in Middle-earth suffer season after season. And sure, the series is willing to kill beloved characters, but it really excels at killing hordes of people and turning entire kingdoms into desolated volcanic wastelands where the sun never shines.

Things are even worse at the start of Season 3, between Sauron trying to forge the One Ring, Mordor's Ringwraiths spreading across Middle-earth, and a Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds) ruling Rhûn. Elsewhere, when it comes to the civil war plaguing Númenor, the realm's only hope is Eärien (Ema Horvath), who was responsible for the King's Men usurping the Númenórean throne in the first place. In fact, Eärien is an unexpected main character early in Season 3, acting as a faithful servant and the head torturer for the usurper Ar-Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) while at the same time operating as a double agent for her brother Isildur (Maxim Baldry) and father Elendil (Lloyd Owen) as they try to restore Queen Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) to power.

Unsurprisingly, things don't go well, as "The Rings of Power" Season 3 kills off two original characters made for the show in its first four episodes. First, Eärien dies in the second episode, followed by the wood elf Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) being tragically betrayed and murdered in Episode 4.

Let's start with Eärien. The character has always felt out of place on "The Rings of Power," with her scenes slowing down the pace and taking away from other, better storylines. Frustratingly, the show simply doesn't have time to cover all the ground it wants to, with the limited number of episodes per season forcing it to jump around too quickly. That being said, Eärien aiding the rise of the King's Men in the secluded and isolated island of Númenor due to her mistakenly believing that following Queen Míriel had gotten Isildur killed was interesting, as was her becoming a double agent once she learned the truth.

Unfortunately, Eärien's double age storyline — her best so far — doesn't last long. By Episode 2, she's already been discovered. So, rather than be subjected to torture and forced to become truly loyal to the King's Men, she dies by suicide by jumping off a balcony.

Likewise, when he was first introduced, Arondir was a great character. Sure, he didn't actually do much, with much of his screen time being dedicated to an attempt at a romance between him and the now-deceased Bronwyn (Nazanin Boniadi). And yet, Ismael Cruz Córdova has always played his role with great gusto, giving Arondir a strong personality that makes him feel like more than just a Legolas knock-off. But that just makes his departure all the more upsetting.

Indeed, Arondir gets little more to do in Season 3 than worry about Bronwyn's annoying son Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin). This all leads to a confrontation in Episode 4 when Sauron orders Theo — now a Ringwraith — to murder the elf. A tragic end, sure, but with little buildup.

With Arondir and Eären's deaths, "The Rings of Power" is quickly getting rid of its original characters. After all, the show had already killed off one of its best brand-new additions in Adar (Sam Hazeldine and Joseph Mawle), while the Harfoots that were so essential in Seasons 1 and 2 are nowhere to be found in Season 3 so far. Granted, Theo's still around, but he's likely to be killed soon as well (due to that whole being a Ringwraith thing). That just leaves Kemen (Leon Wadham), the tiring nepo baby at the center of the Númenor story.

Instead, it's clear "The Rings of Power" is currently more focused on bringing in previously missing characters from J.R.R. Tolkien's source material, like Isildur's brother Anárion (Andrew Richardson) and Middle-earth's own Odysseus, i.e. Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), who's married to Morfydd Clark's elfish warrior Galadriel. It makes sense for the show's writers to be doing this right now, too, as we're getting closer and closer to the end of the series' reported five-season plan. But that means "The Rings of Power" will also have less and less time to explore any of its original characters from this point on.

Another problem is the show's condensed timeline, as "The Rings of Power" is trying to tell a story that spans thousands of years in Tolkien's literature over a much, much shorter period. That means we still have a lot of major "Lord of the Rings"-related developments to get through, be it Elendil and his sons founding the kingdom of Gondor or Celeborn creating Lothlórien with Galadriel. Will all that and more to cover, there's just no more room for the likes of Arondir the wood elf.

#3562. Oksana Baiul Didn’t Have a ‘Choice’ Giving Up Custody of 12-Year-Old Daughter

Olympic gold medalist figure skater Oksana Baiul is defending herself after giving up custody of her 12-year-old daughter in her divorce earlier this year.

Baiul, 48, finalized her divorce from ex-husband and former manager Carlos Farina after 13 years of marriage in January. Per the divorce settlement, Farina was awarded primary custody of the couple’s daughter, Sophia, Us exclusively reported at the time. He was also permitted to move from Louisiana to Las Vegas with their child.

The Olympic champion tagged Farina in a social media post on Wednesday, November 11, writing, “U knew I didn’t [have] a choice! Please make a move from Louisiana as pleasant as possible 🙏🏻.”

“ANY MOTHER Who is going back to reality and rebuilding her future. Understand what is involving to start from the scratch,” she wrote in another Instagram post on Wednesday.

Baiul — who won gold for the Ukraine in ladies’ singles at the 1994 Winter Olympics in Lillehammer — expressed optimism about the future in a post on Thursday, November 12.

“When I look back at that brave 16-year-old Oksana, I see someone who dared to dream and kept going,” she wrote via Instagram, sharing a video of her Olympic triumph. “And today, I promise never to apologize for embracing my worth and being the best version of myself.”

Baiul and Farina’s divorce agreement stipulated that she was allowed to visit Sophia if her daughter agreed to the conditions.

The figure skater agreed to enroll in anger management classes and be tested for alcohol and drugs to “ensure she is remaining sober.”

Farina requested sole custody of Sophia at the time of their divorce, citing Baiul’s alleged history of extreme physical, emotional, mental and verbal abuse” toward him.

He called his then-estranged wife “manipulative, toxic, controlling” and a “compulsive liar.”

In response to Farina’s filing, Baiul accused Farina of being “psychologically abusive” toward her and Sophia.

The couple reached an agreement weeks later that resolved the case.

Baiul broke her silence days after officially losing custody of her daughter.

As someone who makes it a point to watch all the new streaming and made-for-TV holiday movies, including the entire Hallmark Countdown to Christmas lineup, I’m pretty used to plot holes, and they don't bother me much. However, after watching 12 Dates of Christmas, I can’t stop thinking about one confusing plot point: how come Christina’s (Lucy Hale) family didn’t recognize Peter (Ian Harding)?

The premiere of Hulu's 12 Dates of Christmas on the 2026 TV Schedule serves as a mini reunion for Pretty Little Liars fans, as it reunites Hale and Harding for the holiday flick. Hale plays Christina, a workaholic who owns a furniture restoration shop and has made little time for finding her romantic soulmate. After a disastrous family Christmas Eve dinner, Christina makes a promise to herself and her mom that by next year she’ll have someone to bring to it. Of course, the year gets away from her, which leads her best friend (Kahyun Kim) to set up a string of dates for Christina to go on in the twelve weeks leading up to Christmas Eve.

In the midst of the endless stream of disastrous dates, Christina reconnects with her high school crush Peter (Harding), who commissions Christina to refurbish a beloved loveseat for the home he’s remodeling with the help of local mean girl Bridget (Greer Grammer). The two regularly cross paths, and Peter even meets Christina’s entire family when he drives her to the hospital after learning her sister is in labor.

It’s no surprise that Hale and Harding have amazing chemistry and make it easy to root for their characters to get their happily ever after despite the obstacles between them. However, after the infamous hospital scene, I felt myself growing more and more confused as to why Chrsitina’s family seemed to not know who Peter was, considering Christina had a crush on him in high school.

Netflix’s A Dog’s Perfect Christmas Made Me Cry, But Not For The Reasons I Thought

Sure, not every daughter shares their high school crush with their family, but Christina’s family is the meddling type, especially her mom. It doesn’t make sense that they wouldn’t at least know about Peter from her high school pining days. I can maybe believe that they wouldn’t recognize him because he’s older now, but not even getting excited at the name just doesn’t make any sense.

Not to mention, this is a Christmas romance movie, which means the town Christina grew up in and still calls home isn’t a big one. All the more reason for her family to at least recognize Peter’s name, especially since he’s renovating his family’s home.

Ultimately, Christina’s family not knowing who Peter is isn’t that big of a deal. However, I do think it would have been a fun twist if they did recognize him because it would make them meddle in her love life even more. Still, 12 Dates of Christmas is a cute and festive Christmas flick that anyone with a Hulu subscription should definitely check out.

#3560. The Best Ways For Star Trek Fans To Play Magic's New Set: A Guide For Beginner Players

When I sat down at my friendly local game store to participate in a pre-release drafting event for Magic: The Gathering's new "Star Trek" set, several players saw the Enterprise tattoo on my forearm and asked me the same question. If a longtime Magic player wanted to sample "Star Trek," what was the best place for them to start?

Ironically, I was there to ask the Mirror Universe version of that same question: If a longtime "Star Trek" fan wanted to sample the new Magic set, what's the best place for them to start?

I am new to Magic, having only picked up the game a few months ago to prime myself for the new "Trek" release. And one thing Magic and "Star Trek" have in common is that they're both absolutely daunting at first blush. One is a collectible card game with over 30 years of history and dozens of ways to play. The other is a sci-fi universe with nearly 1,000 episodes of television and 13 movies, with dozens of possible entry points.

I can answer one question immediately. "Trek" newbies should start with "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds," with its glossy production values and modern streaming sensibilities, before backtracking and sampling the various other shows and finding the one that connects with their tastes. (This is a sometimes controversial opinion, but I stick by it.)

But the other question involved some legwork, a lot of time spent at a gaming table, a great deal more time sorting through cards, and even a question proposed to the lead designers of the set itself. So, what is the best way for a "Star Trek" fan to sample the new Magic: The Gathering set? Here's what I learned.

One thing I will not do here is explain the rules of Magic: The Gathering, which are intuitive and easy to learn, but challenging to master. There are countless online resources to learn before you try anything I recommend below. I'm writing this piece under the assumption you intend to seek those out on your own.

The best way to truly dive in headfirst is to visit your local gaming shop and participate in a sealed or drafting event. Naturally, this is dependent on your location and whether your local gaming shop is an inviting and safe space (shout out to Mothership Games in Austin, Texas for playing host to my first sealed event). If such a place exists for you, check the calendar and see what's on offer. The good news is that the "Star Trek" set is brand new and there should be plenty of opportunities.

At events like these, players are organized into one-on-one matches and construct their decks from scratch, tearing open booster packs, examine their cards, and trying to build the most effective strategy possible around a 40-card deck. While experienced players will have an edge, they can't bring finely honed and powerful decks from home to immediately wipe the floor with you. Everyone starts at square one. And "Star Trek" fans should take very easily to this format, since the characters you'd expect to be powerful tend to have cards that are powerful. It also leads to some amusing team-ups, like how my winning deck involved an unlikely alliance between Deanna Troi and Gul Dukat.

In a friendly shop with a friendly crowd, this is Magic at its purest: a direct, competitive game where tactics at the table are as important as the strategy behind your deck construction. And the mechanics in the "Trek" set are intuitive and mesh well, meaning that creating a deck that functions as needed is fairly straightforward, and going with your gut choices (i.e., building around characters you like) often leads to strong results.

I can hear your next question: You don't have access to a local shop, or you don't feel comfortable going to one, so what's the best way to play at home? Once again, there are options.

You and a friend (or more) could always buy booster packs, tearing them open and building personal collections and constructing 60-card decks for standard play. However, I would recommend booster packs being the start of your collection, and once you have bought a few, track down single cards to complete your strategy rather than buying more and blindly hoping for strong pulls.

Another option is for you and a friend to buy a pre-release kit, as there are always plenty leftover after the initial week of special event. Use these to construct imperfect but fun starter decks to learn the game, and then grow and expand those decks as you see fit, doubling down on the characters and strategies you're enjoying.

However, the best at-home experience would be to pick up one of the set's Draft Night boxes, which are pricy but offer bang for your buck: enough cards for four friends to craft decks and go head-to-head for an evening, leaving everyone with enough cards to build upon in the future.

However, all of these options require tinkering, and suggest that you'll enjoy the process of building a deck as much as playing one. These options require additional legwork, additional financial investment, and even a bit of luck (although that can be mitigated by buying single cards from reputable online and brick-and-mortar shops). If you want to truly just dive into the game itself and skip the rest of the process, there is another way.

When I had a chance to speak to the key designers behind Magic: The Gathering's "Star Trek" set during a launch event in Los Angeles, I asked if the new set was friendly for "Star Trek" fans with no gaming experience, and if they had a recommendation on where to start.

First, they noted that the set was designed with new players in mind and puts narrative first. A card will generally behave like its counterpart in the "Star Trek" universe, so a fan knows that a Captain Kirk card will be a bit more headstrong and aggressive while Spock will allow for more wily, thoughtful strategy. This means a "Trek" fan should be able to grasp the new cards fairly quickly, using their existing knowledge as a crutch.

Second, they highlighted their recommendation for the best way to sample the game: the "Star Trek" commander decks.

Commander is the most popular format in Magic, where players utilize 100 card decks in four-player games that are slowly paced, socially driven, and generally take an entire evening to play. Think of them as more of a board game experience — or a nerd poker night — than a standard Magic set. Many Magic sets are accompanied by a few pre-constructed commander decks, which players can purchase, open, and play immediately without any prep. The "Star Trek" set has four of them: Federation Fleet, We Are the Borg, Klingon Fury, and Landing Party.

Specifically, the designers recommended the Federation Fleet commander deck as their choice for a "Star Trek" fan hoping to play the game.

Naturally, the next step was to test the designers' suggestion. I rounded up three friends and assigned them each a different Star Trek commander deck, taking Federation Fleet for myself. It's easy to see why this one was recommended: With Picard on the cover and a deck full of '90s "Trek" staples, it's the most popular era of the franchise in one 100-card deck.

Our four-player game took over three hours, and frankly, it was some of the best Magic I've ever played, with all four decks interacting in surprising and wild ways that left everyone at the table screaming and laughing. The "Trek" fans were impressed by the thematic touches, and how the mechanics relate to character personalities and motives, while the Magic players simply relished in the new design elements. I squeaked out a win, but only after the Borg player staged a comeback that essentially wiped out the table. My victory told a story in of itself: Dr. Bashir threw himself at the Borg player, perishing, but in the process, activated his ability to resurrect Ro Laren from the dead, activating her ability and ending the Borg threat once and for all.

After seeing the commander decks in action, I'm inclined to agree with the designers' recommendation. The Borg deck is scary and powerful, but makes them an immediate threat the other players will team up against to defeat. The Klingon deck is pure aggression, which may work against a new player's inherent shyness. The Landing Part deck, with its focus on Original Series characters, is fairly straightforward, but has a lot of moving pieces to consider. The mechanical simplicity of the Federation Fleet deck, and its arsenal of beloved characters, makes it easy to grasp and understand quickly.

Much like with "Star Trek" itself, there are countless ways to get into Magic: The Gathering, and no incorrect way. Ultimately, I agree with the designers: the pre-constructed commander decks, and specifically the Federation Fleet deck, are the best point of entry. Ideally, you'd buy all four and learn with friends for the best possible experience.

But like with "Star Trek" itself, you should be warned: once Magic has sucked you in, be prepared to be sucked in for the long haul.

#3558. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: up to 15 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks when I tested it. The company says some users are finding the latest software update extends battery a bit further.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

Updated 11/10/2026 to note that the Ultrahuman Ring Pro's stated battery life is up to 15 days, not 8-10 days.

#3557. Married to Medicine's Lateasha 'Sweet Tea' Files for Divorce From Dr. Gregory

Married to Medicine alum Lateasha “Sweet Tea” Lunceford has filed for divorce from Dr. Gregory Lunceford after three years of marriage, Us confirmed.

Lateasha, 35, filed for dissolution of marriage at the Fulton County Superior Civil Court on Tuesday, November 10.

The former Bravolebrity stated in the paperwork that her marriage is “irretrievably broken with no hope of reconciliation,” according to court docs obtained by TMZ. While Lateasha did not specify a date of separation, she noted that they split before the filing, the outlet reported.

Lateasha requested spousal support, stating that she “lacks sufficient income and resources to maintain the standard of living established during the marriage.” Additionally, she asked for equitable division of their marital assets and to each keep the cars in their possession.

Lateasha and Greg, 59, met in 2020 after she slid into his DMs. The pair got engaged two years later and tied the knot in Atlanta, Georgia, in April 2023.

“I said what’s up and he responded and from there, you know, FaceTime calls … that turned into a flight to Atlanta, and we met, and we hit it off,” Lateasha told The Daily Dish in 2023, adding that they both knew they wanted to start a family someday.

During season 11 of Married to Medicine in 2024, Greg revealed that he had a two-year timeline for having a baby with Lateasha. The couple explored in vitro fertilization (IVF) in February 2025, although Lateasha, who struggles with endometriosis, later revealed that they had taken a break from their fertility journey.

“Honestly, after getting off the show, we have decided to just really focus on our marriage,” she said in a social media live in October 2025. “At first, I was trying to do it right away, but honestly, with all the drama, I just think that it’s important for us to establish a solid foundation, and of course, like I do want kids.”

Lateasha continued, “I definitely do want a family, but in order to have a family, you’ve got to have a solid foundation.”

Lateasha’s revelation about their family plans came shortly after her exit from Married to Medicine after two seasons.

“Never ever been a quitter. And I never ran away from anybody. It just is what it is. There are better things in store for me,” she said in May 2025. “That platform was what it was at the moment and I think God has something better, and I’m going down the right path.”

#3556. Henry Cavill Comments On Superman Return After James Gunn's DC Studios Exit

Henry Cavill was a great Superman who never got a great Superman movie, and that should have been the end of it. But it's now 2026, and we're still talking about whether Cavill will return as the Man of Steel. With James Gunn and Peter Safran "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads, DC's cinematic future is very much up in the air, and now Cavill is saying he'd always be open to returning as Supes.

During an Inverse interview, the actor was asked if he'd ever play the DC hero again and seemed open to the idea. "Look, there's lots of fantastic storylines," he replied. "There's always a lot of opportunity. As the pigeon sang to Fievel in 'An American Tail,' "never say never." And I buy into that." It's hardly surprising, given that Cavill and his former DC Extended Universe colleague Dwayne Johnson once launched a pretty bizarre attempt to remain in the cinematic universe, most pointedly with 2022's immediately forgettable "Black Adam." At the time, Cavill proudly announced his return as Superman in a social media post following the film's release, but it never actually amounted to anything more than that and left Gunn deeply (and understandably) confused about what was even happening.

Since then, Gunn has introduced us to an all-new Man of Steel in David Corenswet, who made his debut in the charming crowd pleaser that was 2025's "Superman" and is set to return in the 2027 follow-up "Man of Steel." But with Gunn out at DC Studios it remains to be seen where the Corenswet version of the character and his story will go from there. Meanwhile, we've got Cavill telling Inverse he "had such a wonderful time playing Superman in the past" and "would never say never now." It's a bit tiresome, no?

Directly after the extremely perplexing return of Henry Cavill's Superman in "Black Adam," the DCEU collapsed with back to back flops in 2023. Meanwhile, James Gunn was gearing up to launch his DC Universe, which is why the whole situation left him baffled – especially since he was already actively preparing his DC reboot at the time. He wasn't the only one, either. Audiences thought they'd seen the last of the so-called Snyderverse after 2023, but Gunn chose to soft reboot DC with a new cinematic universe that retained elements of the old one. What's more, calls to reinstate the DCEU persist even today.

Now that Gunn and Peter Safran have been removed (er, "stepped down") from DC Studios, it looks as though Skydance CEO David Ellison — who's running the newly-merged Warner Bros. and Paramount — is planning to pretty much dismantle everything Gunn built at DC to prepare for yet another reboot.

Whatever Ellison and his new president and chief creative officer of DC Studios, Jeremy Latcham, have planned for the brand, I think it's safe to say we really don't need more talk of Cavill suiting back up. Had the actor left this character alone following 2017's "Justice League," it might have been a thrill to hear of his possible return a decade later. As it stands, like calls to restore the Snyderverse, this seems to be the discussion that never dies. Perhaps it's that lingering feeling that Cavill never got the movie he deserved, or the fact that Superman remains his best-known character. But for now it would be nice to go a few years without hearing about anything from the Snyderverse era coming back.

The Gen-Z comedy, Adults, dropped its sophomore season on FX and Hulu as part of the 2026 TV Schedule back in August, and since then fans have been loudly campaigning for another season. After months of waiting, the series was officially renewed for a Season 3, much to the delight of the fans.

The cast took to Instagram to share the news with their devoted viewers, which included the reveal that the third season will include 16 original episodes, nearly double the length of the first two seasons. As a massive fan of the show and a firm believer that sitcoms need more episodes, I’m thrilled at the news! In fact, I’m so excited I’ve already compiled a list of things I absolutely need the extended season to feature.

Holiday episodes used to be a sitcom staple, but as television seasons started getting shorter and shorter, these episodes started to disappear. I had accepted the fact that I would never get to see my favorite characters celebrate birthdays or the holiday season, but now that might not be the case.

With a 16-episode season comes space for these beloved one-off episodes. Just think of all the hijinks that could ensue from the Adults gang trying to celebrate the holidays. We’ve already seen them struggle to host a sophisticated dinner party in the first season. Now imagine it’s the holiday season and Paul Baker’s family decides to make the trek to New York to spend Christmas with their son and his new husband after his sister lets it slip that he’s married. The shenanigans would be hilarious!

Over the course of the first two seasons, Adults has found time to include some fun guest stars like actor Charlie Cox, actress/model Julia Fox, and sitcom royalty Raven-Symoné. I’m sure the tradition will continue in Season 3, and I have some ideas on whom the creators should reach out to.

Since Adults films in Canada, it makes total sense that the Gen-Z show should approach a breakout Gen-Z actor who also appears on a hit Canadian-produced show. Yes, I’m talking about Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams. Williams could play himself and act as an old friend from Paul Baker’s childhood, since he canonically grew up in Canada and has a history of befriending famous people without realizing it.

Another obvious, albeit more difficult to get, choice would be New York’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani. I can totally see Issa finding a way to reach out to the Mayor about some minor inconvenience affecting her city that no one else cares about.

Season 2 ended on a major high note with Paul Baker and Anton finally getting together, but it also shocked fans with a plot twist in the final moments that featured Billie and Samir hooking up. Don’t get me wrong, I can’t wait to see Paul Baker and Anton enter their “relationship era,” but I’m also excited to see what shenanigans Billie and Samir get into now that they’ve crossed such a huge line in their friendship.

On one hand, I’d love Billie and Samir to channel the relationship between Chandler and Monica from Friends and try to keep their hookup and subsequent relationship a secret from the rest of the house. It would be difficult considering how close they all are, but definitely worth it to keep it away from everyone meddling.

However, I could also see them trying to act as if their hookup was casual and something they can continue doing without catching feelings. Neither Billie nor Samir do anything without their whole heart involved, so this would be a recipe for disaster but also great for laughs.

Season 3 has so much room for fun and hijinks with its longer episode order, and I can’t wait to see what the writers come up with. While it’ll be a while before the new season is out, fans can stream the first two seasons with a Hulu subscription now.

#3554. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3553. What Did Jason Watford Do? Texas Man Accused of Killing Wife on Cruise Ship

A Texas man is facing a federal murder charge after allegedly beating and fatally strangling his wife inside their cabin aboard the MSC Seascape following an argument on the ship.

Jason Leon Watford, 48, of Tyler, Texas, was arrested on Monday, November 9, after the cruise ship docked in Galveston, Texas, according to the FBI. The alleged killing happened the night before, on Sunday, November 8, in international waters — and a child who was in the cabin at the time was found unharmed.

The woman killed was later confirmed by the FBI to be Watford’s wife, Susan Watford, per reports.

Jason and Susan boarded the MSC Seascape earlier on Sunday before getting into an argument at a restaurant on the ship that evening, he later told FBI agents, per an affidavit written by an FBI task force officer. After the argument, Jason left the restaurant and went back to their room.

Susan followed about 25 minutes later, according to the FBI.

Within the hour, a housekeeper went to the room to deliver towels and knocked on the door.

When Jason answered, the housekeeper allegedly noticed what appeared to be blood on his hands and clothes — and then saw Susan lying motionless, face down on the floor, the affidavit states.

“Security camera footage further showed the MSC employees calling ship security due to observing a motionless female lying face down on the floor,” the FBI task force officer wrote in the affidavit.

Jason was detained by ship security personnel until the FBI responded after the MSC Seascape docked in Galveston.

In his interview with the FBI, Jason allegedly admitted that he and Susan had “continued to engage in an escalating verbal dispute that caused him to ‘snap,’ and he struck [her] multiple times causing blood to emit from her mouth and onto his shirt, pants, and hands,” the affidavit states.

He then allegedly choked Susan with his hands and also wrapped his arm around her neck while she was lying down, strangling her from behind for about four to five minutes until she became motionless, per the filing. FBI personnel reportedly recovered his blood-stained clothes inside the room.

A cruise ship investigator first alerted the FBI to the suspected homicide after Susan was found dead in the cabin “with multiple facial injuries,” according to the affidavit viewed by Us.

The MSC Seascape continued its planned itinerary after Jason was taken into custody, per CBS News Texas.

“We are cooperating fully with the investigation and providing support to those impacted. The ship has left the port and resumed its planned itinerary,” MSC Cruises said in a statement to the outlet. “As this is an active investigation, we cannot provide more details. Our thoughts are with the guest’s family and friends at this difficult time.”

Jason’s court-appointed public defender, Alex Omar Rosa-Ambert, declined to comment on the case when reached by Us via email on Wednesday, November 11.

A child who was inside the cabin where Jason and Susan were staying at the time of the incident was found uninjured, per NBC affiliate KPRC-TV.

“A child was involved in the situation and was found uninjured by the FBI and law enforcement partners,” FBI spokesperson Connor Hagan said in a statement to NBC 5 DFW, noting the unidentified child was “part of the family.”

The child is now in foster care, the Texas Department of Family and Protective Services confirmed to the outlet.

Susan’s foster sister, Breana Chappell, paid tribute to Susan in an interview with Fox 26 Houston, describing her as a devoted mother to several children.

Susan “was a beautiful soul who genuinely brought smiles to everyone she met,” Chappell told the outlet.

“I grew up alongside her, watched her grow into the woman she became, and had the privilege of watching her become a mother,” Chappell said. “And let me tell you, she absolutely rocked motherhood. Her children were her world.”

Chappell added that Susan’s children were “robbed of a lifetime of memories with their mother, and she was robbed of watching her babies become the people she dreamed they would be.”

Jason had a prior arrest in 2024 on a charge of assault causing bodily injury to a family member, according to jail records cited by NBC News. A judge sentenced him to 15 months of probation and 30 hours of community service in connection with that case.

Court records viewed by NBC 5 DFW indicate that the 2024 assault involved Susan, and that Jason pleaded guilty in connection with the incident.

If Jason is convicted of murder in the federal case, he would face up to life in federal prison and a potential fine of up to $250,000.

Anthony Mackie just went on Entertainment Tonight and blurted out the previously unannounced involvement of Paul Bettany in "Avengers: Doomsday." Yep, Vision will re-assemble with Earth's Mightiest Heroes on December 18, 2026, and Mackie probably received a not-entirely-pleasant phone call from Marvel Studios' head honcho Kevin Feige.

"VisionQuest" continues this scene with Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) arriving and lifting the pile of earth off of Wanda. "Scarlet Witch, awaken," says Doom. "Your power will be mine." So, shock of shocks, Wanda is back in circulation.

We know from "Avengers Endgame: Encore" that Doctor Doom has also kidnapped the Hulk, so he's amassing some serious power to wreak a heapin' helpin' of havoc. If Wanda is deep in the thrall of Doom, the only hope the Avengers have of turning her back to their side is her beloved Vision. So that "VisionQuest" reveal should've had every Marvel fan figuring that Vision would play a pivotal part in "Avengers: Doomsday." In a little over a month, we'll know how this all shakes out.
