#3551. Kate Middleton Opens Up About Her Cancer Recovery: “It Will Take Time”

Kate Middleton has spoken about her cancer diagnosis and long treatment journey in a lengthy interview for Country Life magazine, conducted by writer Robert Macfarlane, an author known for his books on landscapes and the natural world. This special issue features Prince William as a guest editor, following in the footsteps of other members of the British royal family who previously served as guest editors for Country Life, including King Charles, Queen Camilla, and Princess Anne.

“I was told in hospital that my recovery would not be linear. There will be good days and bad days, that it will take time,” said the Princess of Wales. As such, her love of nature played a vital role during her treatment. “It shows us that periods of rest, reflection, and renewal are equally as important as moments of growth,” said Kate. This perspective offers a different view of recovery: not as a phase to be overcome as quickly as possible, but as a time when pausing, listening to oneself, and replenishing one’s energy becomes an integral part of the healing process.

In the interview, she also spoke about the therapeutic value of the natural environment, to which she has always shown a particular affinity. “Whether it is the beach for healing and recovery, the countryside for peace and perspective, or the mountains to find solitude, people have long sought comfort in the natural world. It is such a restorative environment, and incorporating nature into someone’s recovery pathway is vital,” she said.

After experiencing illness firsthand, the princess was particularly interested in a holistic approach to treatment and healing. “What I feel really passionate about, having had firsthand experience, is approaching illness and recovery through a whole-person approach. Yes, serious illness creates a lot of physical challenges, but there is also a deeper part to all of us. Nature has allowed me to find a deeper connection to my mind, body, and spirit,” she said.

Kate then explained what she found in the natural environment and why she considers it so precious: “It doesn’t ask anything of us. It doesn’t judge us or expect us to perform. It simply allows us to be.” She continued, “It really has been my sanctuary and a place I’ve instinctively wanted to go.”

The Princess of Wales playing with a little girl

The Princess of Wales reflected on her childhood, recounting how she spent a great deal of time outdoors from a very young age. “I remember from a very early age spending a lot of time in nature, playing in streams, walking in the countryside, blackberry picking, or simply time alone in my own world, enjoying the simplicity of ordinary things.”

Among the memories she shared is one that’s particularly evocative: when she used to dig under bushes, convinced she’d find treasure. A simple game, born of a little girl’s imagination, that transformed a corner of the garden into a place full of possibilities. “There was always a sense of freedom I felt in nature, something about being outdoors that is hard to find elsewhere,” she explained. “When we are little, we seem to notice things more. Like the changing light through the trees, the sound of water, the joy of crunching leaves or finding a feather. These moments can seem ordinary, but, often, they’re the things we remember most. Sadly, this is something I think we lose touch with as adults.”

According to the princess, as we grow up, we risk losing this ability to observe and appreciate the little details. Life becomes more hectic, commitments multiply, and we end up forgetting how important it is to stop, slow down, and pay attention to the little things.

The smiling princess at Chase Community Hospital in Bordon

At one point, Macfarlane asked the Princess of Wales a particularly profound question: Where does she find hope? The writer observed that, in his view, despair is almost a luxury we cannot afford. Kate responded by returning to the theme running through the conversation: the lessons of the natural world. “I find hope in the lessons nature teaches us: that, despite the challenges life may throw at us, we are not alone, and that we are interconnected with something bigger than ourselves,” she said. “We might not be able to have certainty or control every outcome, but we can do the small things, and those small things add up and do make a difference, if we nurture what is around us and have faith.”

Kate went public with her cancer diagnosis in March 2024, after undergoing abdominal surgery in January of that same year. The news shocked the entire world. In September 2024, she announced that she had completed her course of chemotherapy. At that time, however, she had already made it clear that the end of treatment would not automatically mean a full recovery: “Although I have finished chemotherapy, my path to healing and full recovery is long and I must continue to take each day as it comes. I am, however, looking forward to being back at work and undertaking a few more public engagements in the coming months when I can.”

Kate at Chase Community Hospital in Bordon

Kate also spoke in the interview about her approach to motherhood, emphasizing her desire to give her children—Prince George, Princess Charlotte, and Prince Louis—the freedom to explore the world at their own pace and according to their own curiosity. “It is something I remind myself to do with my own children; to give them freedom to explore, rather than constantly telling them what to see or what to think,” she said.

The princess then expressed a specific concern: the rising anxiety among those in younger generations, who spend an increasingly significant portion of their lives online and surrounded by technology. “What worries me is the growing anxiety among children and young people. It’s a generation that’s more online and connected to tech than ever before," she stated. “In this increasingly digital world, I believe it is more important than ever that children grow up with a strong sense of belonging, connection, and emotional security. Nature is a natural environment where those skills can be built.”

Interaction with the environment, she explained, offers children opportunities to practice important skills through hands-on experiences. “Nature also encourages curiosity, imagination, and creativity,” she said. “Whether it’s collecting leaves, building something from sticks, climbing a tree, or simply observing the world around them, children are constantly learning and discovering, about themselves, other people, and the world around them. It is essential for our well-being.”

Macfarlane then linked these observations to the princess’s work on early childhood. He noted that Kate has repeatedly emphasized the importance of the first five years of life and asked her how nature could contribute to laying the foundations for development. The princess emphasized how central relationships are during early childhood: “So much of early childhood is about building nurturing environments that allow strong relationships to grow.”

The princess explained that a child gradually develops various relationships: with themselves, with their parents or caregivers, with other children, and with the world around them. “The natural world gives children an extraordinary environment in which to develop those relationships,” she said. In this regard, she recalled her visit to Reggio Emilia, Italy—an experience she described as particularly meaningful because it allowed her to rediscover many of the principles that guide the work of her Centre for Early Childhood.

Among these is the importance of relationships, the environment, experiences, and, above all, the ability to truly listen to children. “Nature wasn’t another lesson; it offered an integral space that encouraged questions, that stimulated imagination, curiosity, and collaboration,” she explained.

On the very same day the interview was published, Kate visited Chase Community Hospital in Bordon, Hampshire, to learn firsthand about the expansion of a project supported by the Royal Foundation’s Centre for Early Childhood. The initiative aims to help identify more infants who, along with their families, may need additional support during the first months and years of life. During the visit, the princess met with health care workers, professionals, and families involved in using the Alarm Distress Baby Scale, known by the acronym ADBB. This observation tool, which she learned about during her visit to Copenhagen, enables health care providers to identify early signs of social and relational withdrawal in children.

The princess with some health care workers

#3550. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3549. Lauren Graham's 2026 Colleen Hoover Movie Is Officially Netflix's Biggest Streaming Hit

Is there anyone more representative of the recent romance novel adaptation trend than Colleen Hoover? Hollywood loves a BookTok phenomenon, and Hoover's novels seem designed in a lab to appeal to the "crying, screaming, throwing up" crowds on social media, who simply cannot resist what The Guardian called Hoover's "normcore thrillers."

But the film also has some other things working in its favor. For one it stars the talented Maika Monroe, and it also features Lauren Graham, who's best known for playing Lorelai Gilmore on "Gilmore Girls." Graham does a decent job with the material in "Reminders of Him," and regardless of how you feel about the film as a whole, it's nice to see her in a modern-day melodrama.

"Reminders of Him" is directed by British director Vanessa Caswill, who oversaw Netflix's 2023 romantic comedy "Love at First Sight," after honing her chops on BBC series such as "Little Women," "Gold Digger," and "Thirteen." This was another romance movie based on a popular book, and wouldn't you know, the movie went straight to the top of the Netflix charts upon its release. Now, Caswill has done it again with "Reminders of Him," though this one had a successful box office run under its belt before taking over Netflix.

The film stars Maika Monroe as Kenna Rowan, who made a tragic mistake years earlier that landed her in prison. After serving her sentence, Kenna returns to her Wyoming hometown, where she hopes to finally meet her young daughter, Diem Landry (Zoe Kosovic). Sadly, Diem's grandparents Grace and Patrick Landry (Lauren Graham and Bradley Whitford) are completely opposed to the idea. But there's also a strapping young bar owner standing between her and her daughter in the form of Ledger Ward (Tyriq Withers). Turns out Ledger has been helping take care of Diem, and he's similarly concerned about Kenna's return. But as the two get to know each other, romance blossoms, and Kenna finally gets a chance at redemption.

"Reminders of Him" hit Netflix U.S. on November 10, 2026, and according to streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol, became an instant hit. The film shot to number one on November 11, 2026, proving these Colleen Hoover adaptations remain perennially popular. No doubt we'll see plenty more Hoover books being adapted in the near future.

There are plenty of movies to avoid on Netflix, and "Reminders of Him" is right on the borderline. The film managed a 56% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, which is higher than any other Colleen Hoover adaptation. But it also has an 87% audience score, which ties it with "It Ends With Us" for most popular among viewers on the site. Now it has managed to earn the endorsement of Netflixers, does this mean you should watch it?

Well, the movie has a few plus points. For one, it stars the Maika Monroe, who's able to shift from scream queen to swoon queen with ease. Meanwhile, Lauren Graham is given some of the more emotional scenes and does a solid job of bringing them to life. Otherwise, it's sort of okay for the first half? Monroe and her co-star, Tyriq Withers, manage to wring some believable emotion out of the script. Once they throw caution to the wind and just go for it, despite their previous reluctance to besmirch Monroe's deceased husband, everything starts to get a little ridiculous.

Joey Shapiro summed things up quite aptly in his review for the Chicago Reader, when he called "Reminders of Him" a "corny TV movie" that's "made with so much sincerity and conviction by all involved that it becomes watchable, if rarely 'good' by any stretch." If that appeals, or if you simply can't get enough of these romance movies that verge on providing some sort of interesting insight into human emotion only to fall short, then why not give this lesser-known Hoover adaptation a go.

#3546. Did O.J. Simpson Have an Accomplice?

About five years ago, I started receiving a string of increasingly frenzied emails from a man named Todd Guzze. He was trying to clue me into an explosive theory about the most famous murder case in American history: O.J. Simpson had an accomplice on the night he allegedly murdered Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman in 1994. The messages tended to be written solely in the subject line: “Lot of history at VANITY FAIR on OJ CASE…”; “Let me know if you want to chat...” On another occasion, he wrote, “IPPOLITO MOB FAMILY OF NEW JERSEY COVERS UP OJ SIMPSON MURDERS FOR 27 YEARS!! THE REAL SOPRANO’S!!”

The story sounded tantalizing. But my editor and I agreed, after I engaged with Guzze a bit, that given the tenor of his outreach, it was best to leave this lead alone. Judging by the past few weeks, we couldn’t have been more wrong.

A recent New York Times investigation and a separate Peacock documentary, OJ’s Accomplice, each make a more rigorous case for the theory that has circulated among Simpson case obsessives and celebrity conspiracists like Guzze for decades. The foremost additional suspect in this new batch of reporting is Joey Ippolito, a friend of Simpson’s and a drug trafficker turned federal informant who, as Guzze told me in 2021, was connected to New Jersey’s Italian Mafia. (Like the Times, in outlining Ippolito’s larger-than-life biography, Guzze also highlighted Ippolito’s relationship with The Godfather star James Caan.) Guzze has also, to this day, intermittently sent me photos of Charlie Ehrlich, a Miami strip club manager who was convicted alongside Simpson in a 2007 armed robbery case, accompanied by mostly inscrutable theories of Ehrlich’s alleged involvement in the murder. (Ehrlich has not been accused of any wrongdoing in connection with the killings.) The highlight of OJ’s Accomplice is an ostensible hot mic revelation provided by Ehrlich. Following his interview, as he walks to the bar of his strip club, he says, “You didn’t bring it up, so I’m not going to bring it up.”

“I was very good friends with [Ippolito’s] brother Lou,” Ehrlich continues. “Do you know what Lou told me? He told me that a month before Joey died, he took him to Italy…. Joe admitted that he was involved.”

Versions of the accomplice theory have ratcheted up ever since the release of If I Did It, a 2007 book that offered what was described as Simpson’s “hypothetical” account of the 1994 killings.

Guzze has all sorts of theories—he’s also written to me about assorted Jeffrey Epstein matters and a mysterious murder in Utah. Our most extended engagement came in 2024, when he independently published Kim’s Lost Words, a 59-page book billed as a memoir by Kim Porter, the deceased ex-girlfriend of Sean “Diddy” Combs, that has been dismissed by Porter’s friends and relatives as a fabrication. (It ends with Porter, who died of pneumonia in 2018, appearing to predict her own murder at Combs’s hands.) The book rose to the top of Amazon’s best-seller list after Combs was indicted on sex-trafficking and racketeering charges, and conspiracy theories surrounding his sex life and celebrity connections flooded social media. But while that case ultimately fell well short of Guzze’s ideas—Combs was convicted only on prostitution-related charges—I felt obligated, in light of the recent Simpson reporting, to hear his reaction.

“It’s very difficult to watch this happen and to see the world listen to The New York Times and NBC when I’ve already been saying this for seven years,” Guzze told me this week. “Every single news outlet you see right now, every reporter, I already came to them before and they blocked and censored me.” (The broken clock adage comes to mind.) Following the Times’ reporting, a sister of Nicole Brown Simpson has called for an investigation into whether an accomplice was involved in the 1994 murder, as has Alan Dershowitz, who helped represent Simpson during his 1995 trial. While Simpson was found liable for the deaths in a civil suit, according to the Los Angeles Police Department, a lack of conviction in a criminal trial means that the case remains open.

Guzze learned about the accomplice theory from a Los Angeles film producer named Erik Laibe. Laibe, in turn, had learned about it from Ehrlich. Laibe told me this week that he met Ehrlich around the time that Simpson was being paroled from prison in 2017 after serving part of his sentence for armed robbery. They decided to work on a movie telling Ehrlich’s life story, but the project went sideways after the Miami New Times obtained a copy of the script and published a story noting that Ehrlich shared a first name with the accomplice described in If I Did It. “During that time,” Laibe said, “I was contacted by, I’ll say, dozens and dozens of news outlets…and literally from all over the world: ‘Is this Miami New Times story real?’ And I was no comment. The only guy that I called back was a gentleman named Mike Baker.” (Baker and another New York Times reporter, Tim Arango, published the paper’s Simpson investigation last month.)

“One of the challenges early on for us,” Baker told me, “was trying to navigate this world of what is a conspiracy theory and what might be rooted in fact and what are people’s just general theories that they’ve come up with over the years.”

“There was initially a big instinct,” he added, “for people to say, ‘No, I’ve heard this all before. It’s not true.’”

There was a parallel path from these celebrity backwaters to Peacock’s OJ’s Accomplice. “Once I heard the term ‘OJ having an accomplice,’” the film’s codirector Ari Mark told me, “I’m not going to lie, I thought it was really, really juicy and something that I really wanted to serve up to people because I like being part of that energy. But at the same time, it gets you into this weird underbelly of people where you’re not really sure who to believe, what to believe.” For his own dive into the Simpson-adjacent underworld, Mark enlisted Alex Tomé as a consulting producer: a food truck owner from North Carolina and “self-proclaimed O.J. Simpson expert” who had never worked on a documentary before.

“My goal is not to solve the case,” Mark said. “My goal is to say, ‘Can I get underneath this subculture and can I get people to tell me their point of view in a way that feels authentic?’”

I took my own brief dip into the subculture to get a sense of what I’d missed out on by neglecting Guzze’s outreach. Iroc Avelli, a former bodyguard for Simpson, has claimed to have had thumb drives with audio recordings in which Simpson confesses to the murders and says he had help. (Police only found recordings of Avelli talking to himself.) Mark told me that, as he conducted his reporting, Avelli pelted him with antisemitic remarks. When I called Avelli this week, he was less incendiary but just as bombastic, immediately launching into an account of how he first connected with Simpson while he was dealing cocaine.

“I’m only going to deal with facts,” Avelli told me. “I don’t deal with bullshit. I’m not looking to make money off of this because I sold more cocaine than anybody on the West Coast or the Midwest or the East Coast.” He denied making antisemitic comments to Mark, saying, “I’ve been to prison three times; I don’t make careless, frivolous remarks.” He repeated his account that he was certain that Simpson had an accomplice, though he wouldn’t or couldn’t specify who.

These are the sorts of conversations required to produce a story like Mark’s or Baker and Arango’s. Everyone in the Simpson murder orbit, even all this time later, had a harried and sordid quality that made trust difficult to come by. In its way, it was a testament to Simpson’s cultural footprint. I asked Mark how working on his film made him reevaluate the singular personality of one of the most notorious figures in American life.

“I think it reaffirmed my cynicism around optics, celebrity, entertainment,” he said, “and just how far you can fall.”

#3545. 40 Years Later, Top Gun's Most Famous Line Is Still The Greatest '80s Movie Quote

What makes an '80s movie unique? The decade gave humanity lots of horrors that still plague us today, from rampant capitalism, corporations running wild, the rise of the religious far-right, and an obsession with consumerism that is still dominating our lives. But it was also a time of impeccable pop culture, whether it was video games, music, or movies.

Indeed, the 1980s were a wild ride for film fans, with the rise of blockbusters and high concept genre movies with big visual effects paving the way for the IP dominance of the box office. The best '80s movies show the versatility of the medium of cinema, creating strong iconography and delivering one-liners that are remembered decades later.

That's why it's hard to think of a movie that's as quintessentially '80s as Tony Scott's "Top Gun." This is a maximalist movie that exudes iconography, with every exterior day scene being set at sunset, a loud pock-rock soundtrack, plenty of leather jackets, a rousing love of Americana, and old-fashioned American patriotism wrapped in incredibly vague Cold War-inspired politics. This is also a movie so filled with unbridled homoeroticism that it became a gay classic, thanks to a warm story about male friendships that's also so steamy hot that sweaty muscled men are constantly talking about wanting each other's asses while standing half-naked.

Is "Top Gun" the best '80s movie? Probably not, but it is representative of the decade. This movie is an exercise in over indulgence, a movie that's endlessly entertaining and also dumb as hell. The overt military propaganda makes "Top Gun" essentially the movie version of the "Yvan eht nioj" music video from "The Simpsons."

Though the movie has plenty of great lines, one stands out as the most '80s movie quote.

The quote comes early in the movie, when Lt. Pete "Maverick" Mitchell (Tom Cruise) and his wingman LTJG nick "Goose" Bradshaw (Anthony Edwards) are walking down the tarmac on the way to their jets for a new assignment. When a fellow student tells Maverick that his rival Iceman (Val Kilmer) has won yet another contest, the cocky Maverick puts on a fake smile and just replies "I feel the need..." before Goose chimes in and the two say in unison, "The need... for speed!" before doing a high five.

It's a ridiculous moment, a cheesy line with an even cheesier delivery from Cruise and Edwards, but it captures the tone of "Top Gun" — loud, proud, and willing to have fun.

In the context of the movie, however, the line is also important to understanding Maverick. As his call sign implies, Maverick is reckless, and his impulsive behavior makes him a dangerous liability in the eyes of the academy and the military. Sure, Maverick brings results, but he is unreliable, especially compared to Iceman, who is just as good while also being able to follow commands.

"I feel the need, the need for speed" encapsulates not only Maverick's love for danger and for speed but also his insecurities and competitiveness. It's the ultimate expression of American individualism in "Top Gun," the belief of pushing yourself beyond your limits or not giving up when someone surpasses you. It's a declaration of purpose and bravado.

"You are still dangerous. But you can be my wingman any time." — Iceman

"Son, your ego is writing checks your body can't cash." — Stinger

"I don't like you because you're dangerous." — Iceman

"God, he loved flying with you Maverick. But he would've done it anyway... without you. He'd have hated it, but he would've done it." — Carole

"I want somebody's butt, I want it now, I've HAD IT!" — Air Boss Johnson

"You're not going to be happy unless you're going Mach 2 with your hair on fire." — Charlie

Grey’s Anatomy is currently in its 23rd season on the 2026 TV schedule, which is still hard to comprehend. Given that the fans are still tuning in, though, no matter what that hospital has been through, it makes sense. While Ellen Pompeo loves Grey’s Anatomy fans, who have been keeping the show on the air for over 20 years, there is just one thing that annoys her. And I can’t say I blame her.

Pompeo starred in Grey’s Anatomy as the titular Dr. Meredith Grey since the very beginning, before ultimately departing as a series regular midway through Season 19. She’s remained on as narrator and executive producer, frequently returning to the halls of Grey Sloan Memorial in a guest capacity. Having been a staple on television for over 20 years, you’d imagine that Pompeo runs into a lot of fans. Unfortunately, it’s not always the greatest experience. The actress told Magic Radio that even though she loves the fans, she’s annoyed by one thing that would honestly annoy me, too:

To be honest, I’m so grateful for the show and so grateful for the fans, and I love them. But to be honest, when people call me Meredith, I do get a little bit annoyed. So I do get a little annoyed with that. I love that you love the show, but just call me by my right name. And everybody’s so nice, and they just say, you know, ‘I love you so much.’ And so, how really can I be upset at that?

I get why people would call celebrities by their characters’ names. You see them as their characters on television or in movies, and in the moment, you spot them and call them by their signature role. That being said, fans should probably be saying the celebrity’s name rather than their character’s, and I am someone who is a stickler for that. I would definitely find that annoying, because you’re meeting the actual person, not the fictional character. They’re two different people.

For a show like Grey’s Anatomy that has been on for over two decades, I can get why it’s especially annoying as people have had 20 years to Meredith Grey’s actual name. That being said, Pompeo doesn’t seem to have any ill will towards the loyal Grey’s Anatomy fans. Sure, she’s annoyed when they don’t call her by her name, but she still loves them anyway. Folks may just want to be a bit more aware of what they say when they meet Pompeo or any other celebrity and make sure you’re getting the name right.

The actress is not on Grey’s Anatomy as much anymore, but whenever she does return to the medical drama, you never know what to expect. It’s always hard to see a Grey’s Anatomy star leave the series, but in Pompeo’s case, she’s simply not a series regular anymore, but is still a recurring actor. Of course, you can’t have Grey’s Anatomy without the Dr. Meredith Grey, so it’s not like the show could wipe the slate completely clean.

As of now, it’s hard to tell how long Grey’s Anatomy will remain on the air, but there doesn’t seem to be any end in sight. Meaning fans will have plenty of time to practice their hellos to Pompeo if they ever meet her so that they can get the name right. If anything, there are 23 seasons of Grey’s Anatomy reminding you who is starring in the series, so that’s a great place to start, and they’re all streaming with a Hulu subscription.

#3541. Victorian Psycho Review: Maika Monroe Goes Crazy In This Erratic Mix Of Humor And Horror

Horror-comedies tend to lean heavier on the "comedy" side of things than the "horror." But Zachary Wigon's "Victorian Psycho" attempts to do the opposite, giving the audience a gaggle of gruesome, unsettling moments punctuated by wry humor. It makes for an erratic viewing experience — you begin to feel the film would be better served staying in one lane rather than trying to make concepts like dead babies funny. Regardless, "Victorian Psycho" mostly succeeds due to Maika Monroe, who gives everything she's got as Winifred Notty, a psychotic governess who moves in with a wealthy family and proceeds to pile up a body count.

Her attempt at an English accent may be a bit spotty, but Monroe's commitment to playing crazy ultimately works, and works well. Her wry narration guides us through outlandish, blood-drenched moments as she spins a twisted tale. If the film's title (an obvious nod to "American Psycho") wasn't a dead giveaway, it's clear from the jump that Winifred is ... not well. A suspicious past follows her as she arrives at Ensor House, inhabited by the Pounds family.

Winifred may be deranged, but the Poundses aren't exactly a pleasant bunch. Mr. Pounds (Jason Isaacs) is oblivious, Mrs. Pounds (Ruth Wilson) is cruel and ruthless with the staff, and the children Andrew (Jacobi Jupe) and Drusilla (Evie Templeton) have their own issues (Andrew is a brat destined to grow up to be a bully and Drusilla is more than a little creepy). A sane person would take one look at the Pounds family and head for the hills, but of course, Winifred isn't sane.

There's plenty of room for fun here, but "Victorian Psycho" is never confident enough in what it's trying to do. The performances are all very broad and big, save for the always-welcomed Thomasin McKenzie, playing the good-natured but clueless nurse Ms. Lamb, who becomes Winifred's only real friend (and instantly buys into her quickly concocted story about a ghoul roaming the grounds of Ensor House).

As big and over-the-top as many of the elements here are, "Victorian Psycho" also seems to be trying to make a point about the subjugation of women in polite society. Yet it has no real insight into this beyond a surface level approach, and it's hard to get caught up in any sort of message when the film is also constantly pointing out how ridiculous everything here is.

Wigon, who previously directed "Sanctuary," piles on some energetic camerawork that frequently mirrors Winifred's fractured mind, but the script by Virginia Feito, adapting her own novel, relies too much on incessant narration that's not nearly as funny as it should be. And yet, "Victorian Psycho" remains perpetually watchable primarily due to Monroe's performance. A certified scream queen at this point in her career, it's a lot of fun to see Monroe cut loose and swing an axe at people's heads.

"Victorian Psycho" is just a little too unstable for its own good. There's a specific reason why Winifred has shown up at Ensor House, but the slow reveal of what's going on here feels undercooked. And when the film reaches its grand guignol finale, Wigon inexplicably starts pulling punches, robbing "Victorian Psycho" of a more satisfying conclusion and instead attempting something far more serious and dramatic than everything we've seen so far.

What this all comes down to is me wanting to like "Victorian Psycho" a lot more than I ultimately did. I enjoyed Monroe's performance, and the film's morbidly funny atmosphere, but I came away from it all a tad unsatisfied. There's a ghoulish charm to the narrative, but the blood and guts of something far better is lurking somewhere in here, just out of sight.

"Victorian Psycho" opens in theaters on November 13, 2026.

#3540. Why Joran van der Sloot Still Hasn't Faced Charges for Natalee Holloway Murder

Joran van der Sloot admitted to killing Natalee Holloway nearly two decades after he was first named a suspect in her disappearance. He is currently serving time on a U.S. federal extortion charge directly tied to her case, but has never been charged with her murder.

The reason comes down to a single detail of Aruban law: the country enforces a 12-year statute of limitations for homicides, meaning the window to prosecute van der Sloot for Holloway’s death expired years before he finally confessed in 2023.

With Netflix’s Taken: Natalee Holloway docuseries bringing the case back into the spotlight in November 2026, here’s what to know about why the man who admitted to killing the 18-year-old Alabama teen will never face a murder charge for her death.

Aruba’s 12-year statute of limitations for homicide is the central reason van der Sloot has not been charged in Holloway’s case. Because Holloway disappeared on May 30, 2005, the window to prosecute him closed in 2017 — six years before he pleaded guilty to federal extortion charges in the United States and, as part of that plea deal, admitted to killing her.

Even earlier chances to pursue a murder case fell short. Aruban officials reopened the investigation in 2008 after Dutch crime reporter Peter R. de Vries released hidden-camera footage capturing van der Sloot describing Holloway’s death. He was not charged, however, because authorities said they could not corroborate the statements he made in the footage.

Holloway went missing while on a high school graduation trip in Oranjestad, Aruba. The 18-year-old was last seen leaving a nightclub and getting into a car with van der Sloot and brothers Deepak Kalpoe and Satish Kalpoe.

Van der Sloot and the Kalpoe brothers quickly became suspects. They were arrested in June 2005 on suspicion of kidnapping and murder, but released without charges that September. The trio was arrested a second time in November 2007 and again released roughly one month later after authorities said they lacked the evidence to charge them.

For nearly two decades, the case remained unsolved on paper—even as public suspicion of van der Sloot only grew.

While van der Sloot evaded charges in Aruba, he eventually landed in prison for another killing. In May 2010, five years to the day after Natalee disappeared, he was arrested for the murder of Stephany Flores Ramírez, a 21-year-old business student he met at a casino in Lima, Peru.

He was convicted and sentenced to 28 years for Flores Ramírez’s death in 2012. He has been serving that sentence in Peru ever since, with a brief interruption for his 2023 extradition to the United States.

Van der Sloot’s path to finally admitting he killed Holloway ran through U.S. federal court — not Aruban court.

In March 2010, just months before his arrest in Peru, he met with Natalee’s mother, Beth Holloway, and demanded that she pay him money in exchange for information about her daughter’s disappearance. That meeting led to federal wire fraud and extortion charges in the United States.

Van der Sloot pleaded guilty to the federal extortion charges in 2023 and was sentenced to 20 years, which are running concurrently with his 28-year Peruvian murder sentence. As part of his plea deal, he admitted to killing Natalee and agreed to share information about her death.

But that admission came with no additional criminal consequences for her murder. By 2023, Aruba’s statute of limitations had long since expired.

For Natalee’s mother, the long-delayed confession brought a complicated kind of closure.

“My initial interaction with Joran was another moment of, ‘He knows. He knows what happened to her,’” Beth said during a November 9, 2026, Today show appearance, recalling her first face-to-face encounter with van der Sloot upon her arrival in Aruba in 2005.

Beth said she sensed from the start that van der Sloot was responsible for her daughter’s death. It took almost 20 years for him to confirm it.

“I finally have a conclusion,” she said. “There’s a finale. It took me 18 years to get the answers, but justice takes a lot of work, and I felt like now’s the time to tell, for the first time, a comprehensive and conclusive story of what happened to Natalee and her journey of 20 years.”

She described his confession as a day that “was a long time coming.”

“The torturous part is the not knowing, and as shocking and as torturous as it is to hear this, it is finally a relief to know that’s what I had been searching for for 18 years,” Beth said. “I had to know, no matter how brutal it was. I needed to know what happened.”

Van der Sloot has been serving his sentence in Peru for well over a decade—and built a personal life inside the prison system. He met Leidy Figueroa, a Peruvian accountant, in July 2010 when she was visiting her cousin, an inmate at the facility where he was held. The pair married at the maximum-security Piedras Gordas prison on July 4, 2014, when Figueroa was seven months pregnant with their daughter, Dushy, who was born that September.

Reports surfaced in 2023 that van der Sloot had filed for divorce from Figueroa, though neither has publicly confirmed the current status of their relationship.

At the end of Rings of Power Season 2, The Stranger finally realized his name was Gandalf. Now, in Season 3 of The Lord of the Rings prequel, he’s really starting to look like the wizard we know and love. That became especially true in Episode 3, which was part of a four-episode premiere on the 2026 TV schedule, because Gandalf finally got his hat. So, in honor of this monumental moment, I asked Daniel Weyman about putting on such an iconic piece of his costume, and he told me the deeper meaning behind it.

Of course, those of us who love The Lord of the Rings movies associate Gandalf with his robe, staff and big hat. Now, in The Rings of Power, he has all of that. Weyman explained during an interview with CinemaBlend that talking to audiences about this really hammers home the notion that he’s portraying a version of the character Ian McKellen also famously played on screen. Meanwhile, within the story, Gandalf has no clue about the significance and history of that hat. However, it still carries significant meaning to him, as Weyman explained:

What did Gandalf want to do with that hat? Well, he just had this argument with Tom Bombadil, a really serious argument, as it turns out, where Tom Bombadil has disappeared when he comes back. And how does that sit with Gandalf? And then, when this hat magically sort of rolls down to his feet, the final thing, the last vestige of Tom Bombadil in the hut, and Gandalf knows his purpose is to go through the desert, which nearly killed him [in] Season 2.

At the beginning of Season 3, Gandalf is hanging out with Tom Bombadil, and as Weyman said, they get into an argument. After that, the wizard finds The Secret Fire, learns about the other wizards who were sent to Middle-earth, and he becomes aware of the fact that his mission is to help save the Dark Wizard. When he returns to Tom Bombadil’s hut, Tom is gone, and a hat blows over to Gandalf. According to Daniel Weyman, through all this, his character realizes it's time to go back through the desert.

However, there’s more to this. According to the actor, getting this hat is also a symbol of friendship, and it’s part of his armor. Tom Bombadil left this for him, and it helps Gandalf realize his mission and come to terms with the fact that he’s not alone:

He finds that this hat is both a piece of his friendship, but it's also a piece of his armor, and he puts it on. He feels the sun beat down on his head, and he has to put it on because the desert's dangerous. And so, weirdly, in that moment, yes, we're all going to see the outline of it and understand what that means for us, because we know about Gandalf in our world. But for him, he now feels like he's more complete, because he's got another friend to go on a journey with, because he's got another piece of his soft armory.

Weyman went on to tell me that the “key” for him while playing such an iconic character is to “stay present with” his story. He also noted that whether you consider the hat’s history or not, this moment did help Gandalf feel “more complete.”

Now, if you’d like to see how this transformation continues, you can catch the next two episodes of Rings of Power’s third season on Wednesday, November 18.

#3536. Who Plays Thrain In The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3

You shall not pass! This article contains minor spoilers for "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episodes 1-4.

After two years, "The Rings of Power" is back and as sprawling as ever. In fact, it may be even more so than it already was. Seasons 1 and 2 of the Prime Video series took us all over the map (quite literally, thanks to all those nifty map transitions), from the island kingdom of Númenor far in the West to the volcanic wastes of Mordor in the East. Season 3 expands the borders of Middle-earth even further, taking us to new locations and introducing multiple new characters to keep track of — some of whom seem more trustworthy than others.

Somewhere in the middle of all this is the Dwarf prince known as Thráin, the elder brother of King Durin (Owain Arthur) and a figure referenced with no small amount of suspicion towards the end of Season 2. As viewers quickly find out upon returning to Khazad-dûm, there is a fair bit of internal strife going on within the underground city, and Thráin's arrival only exacerbates the tension in the air. While this is actually an original character created solely for the show, he still requires quite a lot of nuance and complexity to fully bring him to life.

So, who better to do so than character actor Eddie Marsan? Yes, it might be incredibly difficult to tell who's actually playing the stoutly Dwarf underneath that mountain of prosthetics, makeup, and that bushy mane of flaming red hair. But, if you take notice of those piercing eyes and distinctive voice, you just might be able to recognize the talents of a performer you've definitely seen before.

As it turns out, maybe there are some Dwarves that you can only trust as far as you can toss them (with respect to Gimli). While watching Thrain do his mischievous thing throughout the early episodes of "The Rings of Power" this season, you'll likely find yourself wondering what else you've seen Eddie Marsan appear in before. In a quirk of scheduling, his most recent high-profile role was actually in this year's "Clayface," where he portrayed Frank Fitzpatrick. As the shady talent manager to Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), this is a perfect example of the kind of slippery character Marsan plays so well. Before that, he popped up in three episodes of the Netflix series "Heartstopper" and had supporting roles in three of director Guy Ritchie's most recent movies: "Operation Fortune: Ruse de Guerre," "Wrath of Man," and "The Gentlemen."

You'd have to go back a little further to pinpoint what might be his most well-known role of all, however. He was cast in the 2009 "Sherlock Holmes" film as the famous Inspector Lestrade, a role he would then reprise in the 2011 sequel "A Game of Shadows" (yes, both of which were also directed by Ritchie). Having worked regularly since the 1990s, the English actor can be seen in a prolific amount of titles over the decades. Some notable examples include Martin Scorsese's "Gangs of New York," the Wachowski Sisters' "V for Vendetta," "Mission: Impossible III," "Miami Vice," "The World's End," "Deadpool 2," and far too many more to name.

In short, Marsan is an acting veteran who knew exactly how to breathe life into a newly-arriving figure like Thráin.

New episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 premiere on Prime Video every Wednesday.

#3535. Mariska Hargitay's Eye-Watering 'Law & Order: SVU' Salary as Lead Revealed

After filming 600 episodes of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, it’s safe to say that star Mariska Hargitay has worked hard for her money.

Hargitay’s character, Detective Olivia Benson, is now Captain of the Special Victims Unit and she’s been top of the call sheet for more than a decade. That accolade and her role as an executive producer means Hargitay now takes home nearly $850,000 per episode, according to Variety.

The actress, 62, has been part of the hit NBC series since its 1999 premiere, making her debut alongside police partner Detective Elliot Stabler (Christopher Meloni).

Once Meloni, 65, exited the series as a regular in 2011 after 12 seasons, the drama became Hargitay’s show to lead and lead she did.

The star has also used her voice outside the series to create the Joyful Heart Foundation, to help change the narrative around sexual assault, something her character would be proud of.

Hargitay’s latest milestone on SVU comes with the 600th episode, airing Thursday, November 12.

“It’s about a woman having her voice and being submissive or subservient in a way, or giving up our power or our instinct, and that’s an important story to tell,” she told Variety about the story line, confirming it will focus on Benson’s personal life even more than usual. “Because so many women identify with that.”

The episode will also feature Meloni as a guest star, which will once again have fans asking why the former partners never became a romantic couple?

“Every relationship is fraught. Every relationship has power dynamics, and will they/won’t they, and what could have been and what isn’t and why, and could they and can’t they, and the complexity of all that,” Hargitay teased of Benson and Stabler’s “intense history” that continued to inform their working relationship.

Ahead of the episode’s premiere, Hargitay reunited with her longtime friend Meloni as well as SVU creator Dick Wolf, Wolf Entertainment chief operating officer Peter Jankowski and the current cast and crew to celebrate their accomplishment.

“It was one of the most extraordinary, meaningful nights, and unexpectedly so to me,” Hargitay recalled of the event. “Dick got up and said, ‘This has never happened, and it will never happen again.’ And everything just landed that night.”

Hargitay also gave a speech that night, toasting to 600 episodes that she said “doesn’t feel totally real — which in a way is exactly how it should feel, because it’s as if we all get to live in this dream of what you thought might be possible someday. And you’ve shown that it’s not only possible, but it’s so much better than anyone could have imagined.”

According to Variety, Hargitay also praised Wolf, 79, and his “television” with the series, saying, “You truly have television — the kind of vision that lets you see and dream and believe far enough and wide enough to create some of this.”

She added, “All those years ago, when you sat there with this idea for the show, and you said, ‘Huh, this might work,’ you used your television, your foresight, to look many years in the future.”

Law & Order: Special Victims Unit airs on NBC Thursdays at 9 p.m. ET.

#3534. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)
