#3517. James Gunn And Peter Safran's DC Studios Exit Was Driven In Part By Cost-Cutting (Report)

It's a bewildering state of affairs over at Warner Bros./DC. After seemingly being welcomed into the newly-formed Skydance (the name of the recently-merged Warner Bros. and Paramount), James Gunn and Peter Safran suddenly stepped down as DC Studios co-heads in a move that came as a shock to pretty much everybody outside of Skydance CEO David Ellison and his colleagues. Now, a report claims the pair's ousting was all part of an attempt to save money, which, considering recent developments, certainly seems plausible.

According to IndieWire, Gunn and Safran's exit was partly "about cost-cutting" as Skydance prepares to tackle its $80 billion debt and deliver the $6 billion in yearly savings over the next three years that Ellison has promised. As the outlet put it, "Skydance has also been stunned by the financial picture of Warner Bros.' film unit," which has struggled to deliver many hits in 2026. We already knew that Skydance had inherited massive flops from the Warner deal (including Tom Cruise's "Digger" and "The Bride!"), but an insider has now told IndieWire that the estimated losses stand at almost $1 billion.

According to the report, this played into Gunn and Safran's dismissal, especially since they oversaw one of the most egregious box office failures of 2026 in "Supergirl." (The Milly Alcock-led movie made just $126.5 million at the box office on a whopping $170 million to $186 million budget.) What's more, sources have informed Page Six that "Supergirl" ultimately lost $135 million. So, while the film's performance was always going to impact whether or not Ellison elected to keep Gunn and Safran in their posts, IndieWire's report has indicated that the cost-saving measures were even more integral to his decision than we previously realized.

After the "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow" debuts in 2027, David Ellison will reportedly dismantle James Gunn's DC Universe, resetting DC's cinematic franchise once again. It's a less than ideal development amid the ongoing superhero fatigue that has already seen the genre fall out of favor with mass audiences. For Ellison, however, it seems the real motivating factor is the same thing as always: money.

What makes Gunn and Peter Safran's exit particularly surprising is that Ellison initially seemed to want to keep them at Skydance. In early October 2026, The Hollywood Reporter cited insiders as claiming the DC Studios co-heads met with Ellison and were asked to stay and "keep doing what you're doing." According to Page Six, however, plans were already in the works to replace the pair with the newly-appointed Jeremy Latcham. One source told the outlet, "It was a little bit strange to have it be so publicly stated that [Gunn and Safran] were safe, and during that time, the [Latcham] process had already been kicked off. They were saying one thing, and then they were actively doing another thing."

But as IndieWire points out, not only was Skydance inheriting multiple flops from Warner Bros. generally, Gunn and Safran's deal was "unusually generous." We already knew the pair were reporting directly to ex-Warner CEO David Ellison, who was seemingly content to leave them to it. But these two were also making a tidy profit of their own, with Safran simultaneously heading up his own The Safran Company and Gunn earning big pay days for producing "Supergirl" and "Clayface," and writing and directing both "Superman" and "Man of Tomorrow." According to IndieWire's insiders, Gunn was making as much as $10 million per DC movie.

David Ellison's post-James Gunn and Peter Safran plans make the cost-cutting explanation even more obvious. Jeremy Latcham, who becomes the president and chief creative officer of DC Studios on December 1, 2026, will now report to Skydance studio heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein instead of directly to Ellison. What's more, one thing we do know about Latcham is that he has a more mainstream sensibility that Gunn's prediction for lesser-known, more off-beat DC properties. What does that mean in Ellison's eyes? A better chance at earning a decent profit when compared with Gunn's plans to give Batman's two most popular Robins their own movie and churn out Mister Miracle animated shows.

Meanwhile, DC Studios hasn't exactly been the biggest money maker under Gunn and Safran. The Man of Steel is one of DC's marquee characters, yet Gunn's "Superman" made $618.7 million in 2025. That's not bad, but for one of DC's most popular characters, it's a little underwhelming (as was the movie). Elsewhere, things have been similarly underwhelming. "Supergirl" was a box office disaster, and the most recent DC release, "Clayface" has done okay, making $111.7 million on a $40 million budget. Bearing in mind this is DC, one of the jewels in the Warner Bros. crown, you can imagine Ellison taking a look at these figures with the weight of his financial commitments and simply deciding to cut Gunn and Safran loose.

For now, Gunn will stick around to oversee the release of 2027's "Man of Tomorrow." According to a source who spoke to Page Six, however, this is only because of Directors Guild of America rules that meant he "could not be removed." If these reports are accurate, Ellison looks to be more intent upon cutting costs than we realized.

#3516. Firefox's New 'Mini Window' Feature Is a Game Changer for Productivity

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

#3515. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3: The Secret Fire Explained

You cannot pass! The dark fire will not avail you, flame of spoilers for "The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 3, "The Secret Fire."

"The Rings of Power" Season 3 does a lot of things right, especially when Sauron is on screen attempting to make a shiny piece of jewelry to master all other pieces of jewelry — all while being haunted by the ghost of Celebrimbor. Indeed, the show shines most when it focuses on the bad guys, like introducing the stunning-looking Nazgnagôl or Adam Young's orc with shifting loyalties and a penchant for poetry.

One thing that is different this season is the lack of mystery identities. We now know very well who Sauron is, we know that The Stranger is actually Gandalf, we finally learn this season who the Dark Wizard is, and we even know why Theo is still in this story. It's as if "The Rings of Power" creators J. D. Payne and Patrick McKay got tired of the waiting around and decided to have god himself come down and explain things directly at the audience.

Well, that is actually exactly what happens in Episode 3, because Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) has an actual burning bush moment and talks to the actual god of J. R. R. Tolkien's Legendarium to learn about the Secret Fire, and his purpose in the story.

In the episode, Tom Bombadil (Rory Kinnear) sends Gandalf on a quest to chase a rabbit. This leads Gandalf to an altar where the rabbit combusts into a flame that speaks to the wizard and explains he is the almighty, whose Secret Fire burns inside every creature on Middle-earth.

Even though "The Rings of Power" is set in a world of magic rings, dragons, dwarves and elves, we have not really seen a lot of thel supernatural — despite it being relatively common in Middle-earth. The world of J. R. R. Tolkien is one of angels and elves that get resurrected, a world that literally goes from flat to round when the creator of all existence gets angry at men and sinks an entire continent to the bottom of the sea.

This is the most overt example of supernatural fantasy we've got in "The Rings of Power" so far, as Gandalf hears a strange voice (Allan Corduner) coming from a manifestation of a flame. The flame gives Gandalf (after calling him by his original Quenya name Olórin) a cosmic vision as the voice reveals itself to be the one who "built the heavens and the stars," that which burns within all living things. As the voice says, "all of Middle-earth is cradled within my flame."

That is the Secret Fire, which is alluded to by Gandalf in the original "Lord of the Rings" trilogy. The Secret Fire, or Flame Imperishable, is Gandalf's higher calling, essentially the power of Tolkien's equivalent of God. Named Erū Ilúvatar, this being is the creator of the whole world, and his Secret Fire is what gives life to the universe. That fire is inside all living beings, and is the thing Morgoth craved most, because he was unable to create life without it, the reason he was driven to the shadow. In Tolkien's world, the Secret Fire is the equivalent of the Holy Spirit in Abrahamic religions, the manifestation of the almighty within all beings.

It is quite funny that "The Rings of Power" has arguably its biggest exposition dump of Season 3 come directly from god, who reveals to Gandalf the entire history of the Istari and reveals the identity of the Dark Wizard. After 2 seasons of audiences trying to work out the identity of the Dark Wizard and his purpose, along drops god from the heavens and just outright explains that he is actually a Blue Wizard and gives audiences the whole backstory in a single scene.

Of course, as shocking as Erū Ilúvatar appearing in "The Rings of Power" is, it makes sense for the show to introduce him now. That's because he has a big role to play in Season 4 and the fall of Númenor. Still, the idea that this show has now officially involved higher beings in the conflict against Sauron is a deep cut concept that separates this from other fantasy shows.

In Tolkien's text, the Valar (essentially the gods of Olympus under Erū Ilúvatar's Zeus) don't get directly involved in the wars of Middle-earth (at least not since Elrond's father convinced the Valar to physically aid in the fight against Morgoth), but their influence and power is felt all throughout the Second Age of Middle-earth and the war against Sauron. "The Rings of Power" leaning more into the supernatural fantasy of Tolkien is one way of making this already quite expansive world even more interesting and complex.

#3514. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. #3513. Marvel Officially Confirms Whether RDJ's Doctor Doom Is A Tony Stark Variant

When Marvel Studios announced Robert Downey Jr. would play Doctor Doom in "Avengers: Doomsday" fans used one word to describe it: desperate. But anticipation for RDJ's return has only grown as "Doomsday" has drawn nearer. Still, significant confusion remains. After all, Downey Jr.'s best-known role is that of Tony Stark/Iron Man in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Now, he's back in that same franchise as a supervillain? It's all a bit confounding, really, and while Marvel Studios head Kevin Feige has just tried to clear it all up, he's also somehow made things even more confusing.

Speaking to Empire, Feige was asked whether RDJ is playing a Tony Stark variant in "Doomsday" or an entirely different character. The Marvel Studios boss seemed to indicate the latter is true. "Is Steve Rogers a Johnny Storm variant?" he said in reference to Chris Evans having played both characters at different points throughout Marvel's cinematic history. "People wondered, 'Is Doom just a variant of another character? Is this just a shortcut to bringing back another character?' The answer is no. He's Victor Von Doom."

Evans played Johnny Storm in a an entirely different cinematic universe, specifically portraying the Fantastic Four member in the 20th Century Fox Marvel movies. He then played Steve Rogers/Captain America in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Downey Jr., however, played Tony Stark in the MCU and is now back as Victor Von Doom in that same universe. Sure, the multiverse has made all of this more nebulous. We saw Evans' Johnny Storm in "Deadpool & Wolverine," which means both he and Evans' Steve Rogers could, conceivably, appear together in the MCU. But it would surely feel like a letdown to bring back the most popular and important actor in MCU history as a villain and let that be that.

Doctor Doom was once Iron Man in the comics, and in 2010's "What If? Iron Man: Demon in an Armor" an amnesiac Tony Stark became the supervillain. But Kevin Feige has seemingly confirmed the Victor Von Doom of "Avengers: Doomsday" is like neither of these examples.

According to the Marvel Studios head, Robert Downey Jr. is playing an entirely separate character to Tony Stark, likely thanks to the multiversal incursions that threaten to collapse the universe in "Doomsday." What we'll essentially see, then, is a character named Victor Von Doom who hails from an entirely different timeline to the main MCU (likely the one that gave us 2025's "Fantastic Four: First Steps"), has no connection to Tony Stark, and just happens to look like the former Iron Man. I feel confident in saying that this only raises more questions. Is there another Tony Stark in Doom's timeline? Is there really no connection at all between RDJ's villain and the Iron Man of the MCU?

Regardless, "Doomsday" directors Joe and Anthony Russo promised Empire that this Doctor Doom will be a truly scary villain, with Joe saying he's "a Gothic character" and "a very powerful character with some very dark magic" who's "not above selling his soul to get what he wants. He's worth being scared of." Interestingly, the co-director added that RDJ's Doom is a "father who's a victim of trauma" and that he has "lost a child." The only parallel there between Downey Jr.'s Tony Stark and his Doom is that the former was once particularly shaken by losing Tom Holland's Spider-Man to Thanos' snap in 'Avengers: Infinity War." Otherwise, he's never lost a child, which is further proof that this is a different character and not a Tony Stark variant.

According to Joe Russo, those who've seen early screenings of "Avengers: Doomsday" have said "it's a very scary movie" due to Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom being "so profoundly damaged." Clearly, the loss of his child is what drives this particular incarnation of Doom — which puts some of the "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer footage in context. In the trailer, we hear Vanessa Kirby's Sue Storm/Invisible Woman saying, "Victor [...] used to be different. He used to be kind, he used to be caring. And then, everything he loved was taken from him." This is obviously in reference to the loss of his child. In that same trailer, Doom accuses all the heroes of having lived "stolen lives," suggesting that something they did in previous MCU installments might have triggered the event that led to his child's death.

Unfortunately, while Downey Jr. did talk to Empire, he didn't shed much light on the Tony Stark variant question. Instead he talked about Michael Douglas at the end of "Falling Down," saying "He goes, 'I'm the bad guy?' I had that realization a couple of days into shooting 'Doomsday,' because all the heroes are over there, and I'm the problem." The actor recalled having "leaned in" to being the villain and having a "glorious time." That's lovely Rob, but are you Iron Man or not? Otherwise, he described Doom as being on a "scorched earth" mission, adding "Whatever you think he may be entertaining, I would ten times it, and you'll probably be closer to the ballpark."

Did Marvel really bring back RDJ without intending to at least hint at Tony Stark's possible return? It seems unbelievable. For now, we'll have to wait until "Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026 to find out.

#3512. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.

#3511. How to farm rupees in Zelda Ocarina of Time

Rupee farming in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake looks a bit different than you might be used to if you played the N64 original or any of its later ports. The most common method in older versions of the game — getting some red rupees above the Castle Town drawbridge — doesn't work anymore. However, there are several other quick and straightforward ways to fill your wallet, whatever size it is.

Below, we break down the best ways to farm rupees in Ocarina of Time remake.

Early in the game, your best bet for rupee farming is scooping up bugs in empty bottles and selling them to the Buyer, which is the man in Hyrule Castle Town who's fanatical about creatures in bottles. He's sitting on the ground across from the Shooting Gallery and slapping the ground with his palms. He'll pay 20 rupees per beetle.

Bugs live under rocks and bushes in various parts of Hyrule, but when you're playing as young Link in the past, the best location to get a bunch of bugs is this spot in northeastern Hyrule Field, near Kakariko Village. You'll notice a Song of Storms bloom, but you can ignore that for now, since the Song of Storms is something you'll only learn in the future. (It leads to a cave with a rupee reward, but it's also full of ReDeads — not a great place for kids!)

Bugs live in the plants and shrubs that surround the Song of Storms plant. Destroy the plants with your sword, scoop up as many bugs as you have empty bottles to fill, and trot back to Hyrule Castle Town to sell them. Repeat the process as often as you want. It's a bit slow, given young Link has to travel on foot, but at least Hyrule Castle Town isn't too far away.

You can keep using this method as adult Link. The Buyer is just in Kakariko Village instead of Hyrule Castle Town.

This method of rupee farming is the most lucrative, but it takes some setting up before you can do it. In the adult Link timeline, the Buyer relocates to Kakariko Village with the rest of Hyrule Castle Town's survivors. He still pays for bugs and fish, but after you visit the Ice Cavern, he'll also buy blue fire off you for 40 rupees apiece.

Make sure you have Farore's Wind from the Great Fairy Fountain in Zora Domain, and clear the Forest, Fire, and Water Temples. Then, unlock the Shadow Temple and learn the Nocturne of Shadow from Sheik so you can fast travel back to Kakariko Village at any point.

With that done, head off to the Ice Cavern, and set a Farore's Wind warp point in one of the rooms with blue fire. Now you can fill all five empty bottles, play Nocturne of Shadow to go back to Kakariko Village, sell them to the Buyer, return to the Ice Cavern using Farore's Wind, and repeat the process until your wallet's full to bursting.

This one's also exclusive to adult Link. No shops are left in the Hyrule Castle Town of the future, but there is a new vendor right at the entrance. They do only one thing: buy Poes. Poes are the spirits that attack you at night in Hyrule Field or any time of day in the Kakariko Graveyard. They leave behind a spirit ball when you defeat them, and if you bottle it up, you can sell it to the Poe Collector for 15 rupees. The graveyard has a seemingly endless supply of them, too.

This method is quicker if you have Epona and learned the Prelude of Light from Sheik after clearing the Forest Temple.

Defeating Skull Kids is one of the more challenging rupee farming methods, but it's also the most lucrative. Defeated Skull Kids drop a gold rupee worth 200 rupees. (It's basically the same as the giant orange rupee from the original game, just not giant. And not orange.) They don't seem to respawn following an in-game timer like other enemies, based on our testing. It appears Skull Kid respawns are tied to real-world time, possibly once per day, though we haven't been able to 100% confirm that yet.

Skull Kids only show up as adversaries when you're in the Lost Woods as adult Link, and they attack as soon as you approach. Skull Kids keep their distance and fire darts at Link, and they're immune to Deku nuts. The easiest way to land a hit is by using the Biggoron Sword thanks to its extended reach. If you take too long to defeat a Skull Kid, they'll vanish and then reappear the next time you enter the Lost Woods.

The quickest way to find Skull Kids is by taking a right as soon as you enter the Lost Woods. You'll find two of them there.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a little bit different than the original game, so if you need guides to help you through, we don’t blame you. We have walkthroughs for all the dungeons, from the Deku Tree to Ganondorf's Castle. We also have guides for the sillier, in-between parts of the game, like when you have to find Richard (the dog) or Cuccos.

For those going for 100% completion, we also have guides on where to find every Piece of Heart, every Gold Skulltula token, and where to plant every Magic Bean.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3510. Avengers: Doomsday's Official Writing Credits Confirm Two Major Marvel Cameos

As the December 18 release of "Avengers: Doomsday" rapidly approaches, fan speculation is running rampant over just about every aspect of the movie. Is Doctor Doom a Tony Stark variant? Which characters will die? And who will make surprise cameos? Anthony Mackie recently spoiled the return of Paul Bettany's Vision, while there's also been talk that the finalized Writers Guild of America writing credits would tip the appearances of two hugely popular characters. This talk is now fact.

Those credits are now official, and, per the WGA website, Stephen McFeely and Michael Waldron will share the coveted "written by" credit (with an "and" instead of an "&," which means they did not write as a team). Meanwhile, quite a few folks received Additional Literary Material credits (which will not be seen on screen). Here's the list: McFeely, Waldron, Eric Pearson, Chris McKenna, Erik Sommers, Jeff Loveness, Andrew Lanham, Destin Daniel Cretton, Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman.

Yep, the previously uncredited Reynolds and Jackman will join the spandex showdown as Deadpool and Wolverine. Probably. I mean, it'd be funny if the fellas were hired to punch up Kelsey Grammer's dialogue, but, no, this almost certainly means the indestructible duo is back. As for how significant a role they'll play in "Avengers: Doomsday," your guess is as good as mine. So let's get to guessin'!

My greatest fear regarding "Avengers: Doomsday" is that it'll be undone by superhero clutter. If the Russos don't have a compelling story (and we know they began shooting without a finished script), it could be a comic book version of those leaden 1960s all-star romps like "Casino Royale," "Candy" and "The Magic Christian," where each actor's sole function is to pop up on camera so the viewer can say "Hey, there's Orson Welles!"

I've been encouraged by some of what I've heard over the last month – in particular, that James Marsden's Cyclops plays a significant role in the film. If this means we'll get a resumption of hostilities between the humorless Scott Summers and cocky Logan, I'll be so very happy. Add the exponentially more antagonistic Deadpool into the mix, and that just may be enough to drive Summers into the steely arms of Doctor Doom.

I'm most excited to see Deadpool be the straw that stirs the drink. I really don't want a relentlessly dour "Avengers: Doomsday," which is the vibe I'm getting from the pea green aesthetic of the trailers (and its fast food tie-ins). Are they going to get MCU fans to buy back in with a surfeit of character deaths? Gunn's "Superman" caught on because it foregrounded hope in a thoughtful, non-anodyne way. We live in bleak times. I'm not sure AI-friendly filmmakers like the Russos should be in charge of a franchise that, overall, appeals to our sense of humanity. I'm hoping the heavy-handed trailers are a happy bait-and-switch. Let Deadpool and Wolverine cook.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe are down to $199 from $359 ahead of Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet, according to price trackers. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

#3508. Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before

Few human emotions are as fathomable as grief. Someone (or something) was here, had meaning and value and presence, and is now gone. There is a hole, a gap, an empty space. The pain that accompanies that void may manifest in different people in different ways, but its very existence is understandable. What makes people happy? What makes them sad? What makes them angry? Grief, well, that’s an easier question with a tougher answer.

For her third feature film, German filmmaker Sandra Wollner tackles the most tangible of dramatic genres — the grief tale — and turns it on its head in a way that our own David Ehrlich called “infinitely beguiling.” Mostly, the film shows how infinitely elastic and malleable this genre is, and the emotions that power it. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies Democrats Won. When Do Hollywood Crews Get Back to Work?

The logline for the Un Certain Regard winner is simple enough: after the death of teenager Jessie (Carla Hüttermann), her mother Ella (Birgit Minichmayr), her little sister Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling), and her boyfriend Lux (Tristán López) form an unlikely family unit as they attempt to move on. To say much else is spoiler-y in the truest of senses: It would detract from the joy and wonder of watching this story unfold.

That Wollner’s film is doing something different with seemingly well-trod material is obvious from the start, as “Everytime” layers on cut scenes from the video game “Vintage Story” — not “Minecraft,” though Wollner understands why the audience might think it’s the more well-known game — long before the real drama kicks in.

A familiarity with “Vintage Story” is not required to understand her film, Wollner promised during a recent interview with IndieWire. “Maybe if someone hears the dialogue of Melli and Lux, then maybe they would feel they have to know more about it, because they’re talking about how you can basically cut trees to harvest stuff and to get that, but I don’t feel that you have to know anything,” she said.

Wollner herself isn’t even a “hardcore gamer,” but she admires video games for their world-building and how they can encourage exploration. Her early forays into both “Vintage Story” and “Minecraft” tickled that. “It felt like the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon, but before the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon,” she said. “You’re walking through infinite worlds that feel so big, but minimalistic in a way. And the sounds; a very ambient sound feels eerie and soothing at the same time. I was just very compelled and inspired by that.”

The idea that Jessie would leave behind her own video game world that Melli could then play in was one of the film’s first seeds. “I thought, it’s a way of a memorial I haven’t seen so far,” she said. “[We have this] whole world of avatars and gaming communities where people meet online and then if someone really goes out, their avatar might live forever in there and create a life on its own in a way. I just found that very intriguing, and this is why I wanted in there.”

While the film is unique in how it handles digital mementos — avatars, literally — Wollner also pays close attention to real-world details that can make grief feel even bigger.

“One of the first scenes [I thought of] was Ella lying down on the couch and hearing how her daughter would come back [into their apartment],” the filmmaker said. “It’s something I think also everybody can relate to, even with a more natural loss and not such a tragic one. For example, when I was a kid, my aunt would always run down the stairs [in the apartment complex where we lived], and I would always hear her in the morning, running down in the morning. The noise was very specific to this person. I didn’t want it to be full on, but to let us think, it couldn’t be Jessie.”

Wollner was also intrigued early on by the “constellation of people” impacted by the loss of one. “The boy, the little girl, and the mother, it’s people I’ve met in my life in several decades, I would say, variations of them, but somehow similar constellations,” she said. “They seemed very clear to me. Three people who, especially the mother and the boy, really tried to do the right thing in a way. But there is a big conflict in there. They are having a weird dependent relationship. She needs him to grieve. He needs her to forgive. Of course, I could have made this conflict much bigger, but I really was interested in ordinary people who just try to do the right thing and just try to go along with that.”

Having her own child added a new dimension to the film, even for Wollner. The filmmaker was editing the film when her daughter was born (her longtime partner is writer and cinematographer Timm Kröger, who also worked on the digital imaging in “Everytime”), an experience that deepened her understanding of her own work.

In the film’s second half, the trio travel to Tenerife, Spain on holiday, a place that baby Jessie (who we’ve seen in home videos) once visited. There, they discover another baby, who looks just like Jessie, playing happily in the same quiet space that baby Jessie once occupied.

“We watched the scene again of baby Jessie sitting there, and we looked at each other,” she said. “I always understood what [that scene] means for me, but there, we really felt it for the first time, being a parent. And I felt, oh, I really nailed it! I mean, that sounds so stupid, but when I had the baby, I think, as many people feel, you still sometimes have the feeling, oh, where does it come from? It’s suddenly here. Suddenly there’s a person there. It’s like with that moment when she walks around the corner, and baby’s sitting there.”

Wollner was also compelled by the way we memorize different places and the unpredictability of memory. The odd little space, located in the far reaches of the resort’s clubhouse, comes to haunt Ella, Melli, and Lux in different ways, forever linked to Jessie and her absence.

“When my dad died, I was with him, and I suddenly had this image of him standing somewhere in this bend on the river and fishing, and it felt so familiar,” the filmmaker said. “This memory intruded on my present. We cannot control when we get a memory. They’re just coming. Sometimes we can make them happen to come. But we never know if maybe the weird place where we saw our baby sitting or the weird moment is the one that haunts us the most. It’s this weird banal little room with this weird banal kitschy toy that is playing this music. And this is the thing that then comes back.”

Those “banal little” details pack immense emotional power. So do turns from Minichmayr and López, who never turn to over-the-top histrionics to convey their grief. Wollner’s choice to set the majority of the film a year after Jessie’s death helped, giving the characters some distance from the immediate stab of loss.

“It was a conscious choice to pick some time after the death [to mostly focus the film on],” she said. “As a writer, we need to know what happened in the time between, and so I wrote that as well, but it honestly felt not depictable. I feel I can only fail to show that. I wasn’t interested in these big emotions. That just felt too overwhelming. And sometimes we are made to believe that grief comes in these neat boxes to check: Now you’re sad, now you’re angry, now you accept. Maybe you can be angry again, then you accept. It’s just this messy thing that you can feel for a very long time.”

Keiling also offers a nuanced performance, built more on a kid’s curiosity than on saddling the young actress with big, showy scenes. There’s no screaming and crying here, no sobbing or yelling. But that doesn’t mean that Keiling wasn’t accessing some major emotions.

“I love to work with kids,” Wollner said. “And even having a kid, I think I still am a kid in a way. For this one, I met Lotte, I had not met another kid, I only met her, I did not do any other castings. I just fell in love and thought, oh, she’s exactly what I thought of Melli could be and even better, so I trusted the script to her.”

Wollner worked with fellow filmmaker Juli Neuhaus, who served as a “kids’ coach” for the younger members of the cast. Wollner and Neuhaus were eager to meet Keiling where she was. The young performer loves to draw, so she would draw the scenes before performing them, to better understand what they were about, which allowed her to access a full spectrum of feeling.

“With Melli, there was no scene where she really had to act her grief,” she said. “I always felt that the film itself, the editing and the framing, the absence, we see her doing her homework, and then we see the same room behind her, but now we know that the sister is not there anymore, I always felt that this will tell us the grief, so she doesn’t need to act it. If she holds her phone and is texting her sister, it will already make us feel the grief. She doesn’t need to feel the heavy weight of that. So, actually for her, it was, I would say, like a very light shoot. Playful. It was really playful.”

Still, for all its sense of fantasy and play, “Everytime” is about a terrible heartbreak. Yet, as ever, Wollner chose to depict Jessie’s sudden, shocking death in a unique way, tracking her fall from a tall building while out with Lux from a great distance away. We can see it. We can do nothing about it. That’s grief, too.

“This was one that really was clear to me in the writing process already, that we’re going to have this lens and that we have this weird perspective of the universe itself looking at it, being so far away and still not able to do something about it, but still witnessing so intimate,” she said.

The actors were on one high-rise building, while Wollner and her crew were on another, about half a mile away. “And we had this insane lens. I had a 3,000-millimeter consumer camera, which is an insane lens,” she said. “It’s really like you don’t want to point it on people. It feels really not OK. But I was sure that I wanted to work with exactly that length or something similar to that, that feels kind of forbidden to be so close and too far away at the same time.”

While the scene is shot as if Jessie and Lux are very close to the edge of the building, the actors were not. (Hüttermann later told Wollner that she still had the feeling she might fall, even with myriad safety measures in place. That’s just how immersive the entire thing felt.) Hüttermann’s actual fall was shot in a studio, and their visual effects supervisor Kariem Saleh combined that footage with the outdoor shots.

Because they needed a certain kind of light, Wollner estimated they had only about five takes to get it right, though she knew they would likely only get one shot with the “perfect” light. Her script also called for the camera to follow a bird after the fall, but she said with a laugh, “Unfortunately, no bird came in exactly that moment.” (They lensed other birds, though, and those also ended up in the final composite shot.)

“We worked so many hours just on the sounds, just to get the right level of there is a little sound, and there is a little tink when she falls down, a little bit,” she said. “Just to realize, given how far away we had to be, how does the sound have to be? We worked the whole time on that, and I never really felt it until I sat at Cannes in the audience. And I heard the gasps for the first time and really it went through my bones. I mean, it’s weird to say that, but I was happy, but I felt the first time that it actually worked.”

Wollner remains very emotionally connected to the film, constantly talking about the way certain scenes make her feel, either while making them or editing them or even seeing them with an audience. Of course, such a deep-feeling filmmaker crafted such a beguiling film, one that invites all sorts of responses and theories. Since Cannes, audiences have been talking about its genuinely thrilling third act and the implications of its final scenes. And while we won’t spoil them here, we had to ask: What did Wollner want her viewers to feel in those moments?

“The feeling that I wanted to have is that [this film that is] grounded or hopefully grounded in the beginning, then suddenly you walk around the corner and you feel still some ground, but it’s such an odd place now and you don’t know,” she said. “I always hoped it doesn’t feel just dreamy, but there is some groundedness to it and that the people still react in a way that made sense for them, the characters, but that you don’t know what room you entered now, some kind of back room. That was clear from the beginning.”

And, as fantastical as it might sound, she’s clear: it’s all real. “I mean, it’s such a cliché to say that, but everything we see at the end is true at the same time,” she said.

A 1-2 Special release, the film is in limited theaters now, with a wide release to come in February 2027.

#3507. Rings Of Power Season 3 Features The Most Gruesome TV Scene Of 2026

The land of Mordor is where the shadows lie, and this article is where major spoilers lie. Read no further if you haven't watched the Season 3 premiere episodes of "The Rings of Power."

"The Rings of Power" is a tragedy. As far as prequels go, this one is not as full of doom and gloom as "Andor" — a show where audiences knew the main character was destined to die tragically — but it is still a show all about the rise of an evil that almost conquered Middle-earth. Indeed, though there are some surprising main characters in Season 3, the true star of "Rings of Power" is the Dark Lord Sauron (Charlie Vickers), who spends each season lying and manipulating his way to ruining everyone else's day.

This was especially prominent than in Season 2, which was all about Sauron making the elves believe he was an envoy of the Valar so that they'd help him make the titular Rings of Power. In particular, Sauron spent the entire season gaslighting the show's best and most tragic character, Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards). Episode after episode, Sauron used Celebrimbor's vanity and pride to his advantage, scheming and lying into making Celebrimbor his friend and ally, before stabbing him in the chest with a pike.

This leads to "Rings of Power" Season 3 featuring the most gruesome TV scene of 2026. When Sauron returns to his little office in Barad-dûr after failing to make the One Ring yet again, the Dark Lord gets a visit from the ghost of Celebrimbor, who mocks Sauron's failures at trying to replicate the dead elven smith's work.

And right there, in front of Sauron, is the rotting body of Celebrimbor, hanging on a wall like a trophy.

What makes this horrifying is not only that Sauron still keeps the dead body of Celebrimbor around, but the fact that it's a rotting mess with arrows sticking out of the torso. Making matters worse, Skelebrimbor is hung from a wall like a war banner

This, of course, is a reference to the actual books. As J.R.R. Tolkien himself wrote, Celebrimbor's dead body was "hung upon a pole, shot through with Orc-arrows" and turned upon Elrond's forces like a banner for Sauron's army. It's why fans affectionately refer to this act as "Celebrimbanner." It is arguably one of the cruelest things the Dark Lord ever did — which is saying something considering the untold number of people that died because of him.

Seeing the body of Celebrimbor hanging on a wall — the flesh rotting away, an expression of fear and shock on the skeleton — is horrifying, and easily the most gruesome piece of imagery in the entire "Lord of the Rings" franchise. There is no reason why Sauron needs to have kept the body of Celebrimbor, other than to assert his cruelty.

And yet, it leads to a rather hilarious scene of the ghost of Celebrimbor appearing only to taunt Sauron, ragebaiting the Dark Lord and mocking his inability to craft anything as majestic as the great smith Celebrimbor. He even tells Sauron that his orcs now pity him because of how pathetic his jewelry crafting skills are. It's a testament to Charlie Vickers for the subtle ways in which you can tell the insults are actually getting at Sauron. Meanwhile Charles Edwards reminds us why he is one of the best pieces of casting in this show, with this short but impactful scene in a third season that otherwise struggles to live up to hype.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

#3505. Ghost Rider Star Says He's Down to Return for Marvel's 2028 Reboot

Marvel Studios is bringing back the supernatural hero Ghost Rider in a new movie in 2028, with Ryan Gosling in the lead role. Exactly which version of Ghost Rider Gosling will tackle remains unclear, but one former actor who donned the flaming skull says he's down to ride alongside the rebooted silver screen Spirit of Vengeance if Marvel calls: Agents of SHIELD star Gabriel Luna.

In an interview with Polygon, Luna said, "If they call, I'll do it."

Speaking with Luna for Dexter: Resurrection season 2, Polygon's Jake Kleinman asked The Last of Us and Terminator: Dark Fate actor for his reaction when Marvel announced the new Ghost Rider at this year's San Diego Comic-Con.

"I was excited," Luna said. "I think it’s gonna be pretty awesome. I like [director] Shawn Levy. [...] It’s gonna be really, really exciting."

Luna portrayed the Roberto "Robbie" Reyes version of Ghost Rider in season 4 of Agents of SHIELD, which aired on ABC from 2016–2017. Reyes was the fifth character to be named Ghost Rider in Marvel Comics, and was introduced in the pages of All-New Ghost Rider in 2014. For the past decade, Luna said, he's received plenty of questions about reprising the role.

"First of all, I love and appreciate everybody who loves Robbie and how they keep asking here after 10 years," he said. "Eventually they wore me down. I was like, 'All right, fine. If they call, I’ll do it.' You gotta stay open to all these types of things. And the story is number one. And if there’s a reason for Robbie to ride side by side with Ryan’s Ghost Rider, then there’s a reason to do that. But otherwise, I’m gonna love and enjoy the continuation of one of the most iconic and the greatest characters in Marvel lore."

Luna said he doesn't have any insider info on which version of the character Gosling would play in Ghost Rider — reportedly, it's Johnny Blaze — but has one hopeful take in mind: "I don’t know who he’s gonna play. I kinda hope it’s Danny Ketch. But yeah, I’m gonna be front row when it all goes down," he said.

Gosling will be at least the fourth actor to portray a Ghost Rider in live-action, following Nicolas Cage's role as Johnny Blaze in 2007's Ghost Rider and its 2012 sequel Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance; Sam Elliott as Carter Slade in Ghost Rider; and Luna in Agents of SHIELD. (Incidentally, two other actors on that TV show were also briefly possessed by the Spirit of Vengeance: Clark Gregg and Henry Simmons.)

Marvel Studios' Ghost Rider is slated to arrive in movie theaters on July 28, 2028.

#3504. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

#3503. 5 Best TV Shows Like The Good Daughter

This article contains discussions of addiction, domestic violence, mental health, and sexual assault.

There's a new dark crime thriller on Peacock, and if you haven't watched "The Good Daughter" yet, prepare yourself — this show is unrelentingly distressing, but it'll keep you captivated from beginning to end.

Two of film and television's most talented actresses, Meghann Fahy and Rose Byrne, lead this series — based on a book by thriller writer Karin Slaughter, who also created the show — about sisters Charlotte and Samantha Quinn, respectively. As teenagers, Charlotte and Samantha endure a horrifying tragedy when their mother is shot and killed in front of them in their home by masked intruders, after which both girls are also attacked. Years later, Charlotte is working in their hometown of Pikeville, Georgia, with their father Rusty (Brendan Gleeson), a defense attorney whose work may or may not have caused the home invasion that killed his wife and the mother of his children, and Sam lives in New York City as a patent attorney who's trying to escape her past. When a new tragedy strikes in Pikeville and Charlotte gets a front-row seat to the carnage, the sisters reunite under difficult circumstances, unpack their family trauma, and ultimately work together to prove that a teenage girl is innocent.

If you finish binge-watching "The Good Daughter" and want to keep the crime drama streak going, I've got some follow-up suggestions for you. You may notice that "Pieces of Her" and "Will Trent," two other high-profile Slaughter adaptations, don't appear here; the former just barely missed the cut in favor of some other picks, and the latter is very tonally different (largely because it's a network drama). Check your trigger warnings and then try out these five shows you'll like if you loved "The Good Daughter."

Gillian Flynn's most famous novel might be "Gone Girl," which got an incredible film adaptation, but don't sleep on her debut novel and its small-screen adaptation. "Sharp Objects," which dropped on HBO in 2018 and was helmed by the late, great Jean-Marc Vallée and "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" alum Marti Noxon.

After a girl goes missing in her hometown of Wind Gap, Missouri, in the aftermath of a different young woman's murder, journalist Camille Preaker (Amy Adams) — who struggles with serious trauma, her mental health, compulsive self-harm, and an alcohol addiction — reluctantly goes back to Wind Gap and reunites with her controlling Southern belle mother Adora Crellin (an imperious, perfect Patricia Clarkson). When the missing girl's body is discovered shortly thereafter, Camille attempts to solve the murder, tangling with big city detective Richard Willis (Chris Messina, reuniting with Adams after their much less intense film "Julie & Julia") as well as her impulsive and rebellious younger half-sister Amma Crellin (Eliza Scanlon).

Vallée and Noxon create an airless, claustrophobic environment in Wind Gap as Camille tries to face her demons head-on and figure out who's responsible for the deaths of multiple girls ... whose bodies are often missing teeth when they're found. With an ending that'll leave your jaw on the floor and a performance from Adams that should have, by all rights, handed her an Emmy — to say nothing of the magnificent turn from Clarkson — "Sharp Objects" is a must-watch no matter what. Its themes of family trauma pair perfectly with "The Good Daughter."

Philadelphia local Brad Inglesby, who's also the mind behind "Task," created and wrote "Mare of Easttown," which is set in a fictional suburb of Philly called Easttown and hit HBO in 2021. (Confusingly, there is a Philadelphia suburb called Easttown, but it's not the one depicted in the show. Try to keep up!) Kate Winslet stacks accent upon accent as the titular Marianne "Mare" Sheehan, a local detective tasked with investigating the murder of a young single mother, as she continues to try and track down a different missing girl whose case has gone mostly cold. On top of all of that, Mare tragically lost her son years prior, and she lives with her own guilt and grief every day as she also tries to deal with her surviving family, especially her difficult mother, Helen Fahey (Jean Smart), and provides support for her best friend, Lori Ross (Julianne Nicholson).

As Mare teams up with county detective Colin Zabel (a phenomenal Evan Peters, who really nails this tricky accent), struggles to parent her rebellious daughter Siobhán (Angourie Rice) with her ex-husband Frank (David Denman), and tries to solve the murder of said single mother Erin McMenamin (Cailee Spaeny), she also has to deal with her own trauma. Like in "The Good Daughter," Mare's past frequently gets in her way as she attempts to deal with her present, and like "The Good Daughter," the ending of "Mare of Easttown" is as satisfying as it is devastating and sobering. Speaking of "Task," by the way, the shows are set in the same universe ... and Nicholson actually reprised her role as Lori on Inglesby's other series in 2026.

Liane Moriarty has been writing exceptionally sharp and deceptively dark thriller novels for decades now, but thanks to a high-profile adaptation of her 2014 novel "Big Little Lies" in 2017, that book is arguably her most popular by a mile. Jean-Marc Vallée also worked on this series (which was created by David E. Kelley), which moves the novel's story from a ritzy neighborhood in Australia to an exclusive and wealthy community in Monterey, California, populated by mothers like Madeline Mackenzie (Reese Witherspoon), Celeste Wright (Nicole Kidman), and Renata Klein (Laura Dern). When newcomer Jane Chapman (Shailene Woodley) moves to town with her precocious son Ziggy (Iain Armitage), Madeline and Celeste welcome her into the fold with open arms, and as the women bond, it's revealed that they're all struggling in various ways.

Madeline is remarried to Ed (Adam Scott) but shares a daughter, Abigail (Kathryn Newton), with her ex-husband Nathan (James Tupper) ... whose new wife, Bonnie (Zoë Kravitz), irks Madeline to no end. Renata's daughter has been hurt by someone at school, and she blames Ziggy, but the culprit remains at large. Celeste's handsome husband Perry (Alexander Skarsgård) seems perfect, but he's physically abusive behind closed doors; as for Jane, she suffered a devastating sexual assault that resulted in Ziggy but still haunts her years later. As the women's stories converge in entirely unexpected ways, all their problems hit a crisis point ... but they stick together under duress. Yes, the second season of "Big Little Lies" was terrible, and I'm extremely apprehensive about the third season that's in the works — but as far as that first season that was intended as a miniseries, it's unimpeachable and completely complementary to "The Good Daughter."

Another deliciously dark drama that's exclusively available on Peacock, "All Her Fault," adapted from a novel by Andrea Mara, opens as working mother Marissa Irvine ("Succession" veteran and Emmy winner Sarah Snook) goes to pick her young son Milo (Duke McCloud) up from a playdate with a new friend at school. When she gets to the house, she's met by an older woman who's never heard of Marissa or Milo, and before long, Marissa discovers that Milo is missing. After frantically calling her husband Peter (Jake Lacy), the search for Milo begins, and even with her best friend and business partner Colin Dobbs (Jay Ellis) and Peter's troubled but well-meaning sister Lia (Abby Elliott) by her side, Marissa feels adrift and understandably terrified. That's when she turns to her fellow working mother Jenny Kaminsky (Dakota Fanning), who not only understands what Marissa goes through every day as a woman attempting to juggle work and motherhood, but is an invaluable source of support during the most frightening time of Marissa's life.

It's a credit to the bones of Mara's story that, even in its most heightened moments, "All Her Fault" manages to avoid melodrama or absurdity; in fact, it's really grounded by Snook's emotional but intense performance, and Lacy, Fanning, Elliott, Ellis, and supporting players Michael Peña and Sophia Lillis also turn in absolutely incredible performances as a detective and Jenny's nanny, respectively. "All Her Fault" shares a lot more with "The Good Daughter" than a streaming platform — long-held family secrets play enormous roles in both shows — and it's a perfect follow-up.

"The Better Sister," which has a home on Amazon Prime Video, is adapted from a novel by Alafair Burke and premiered in 2025 with showrunner Olivia Milch at the helm. The premise is simple but deeply unsettling: Magazine editor Chloe Taylor (Jessica Biel) is happily married to Adam Macintosh (Corey Stoll), but when he's murdered, she's forced to reunite with her troubled sister and Adam's ex-wife Nicky Macintosh (Elizabeth Banks) as the two try to figure out what happened.

The two lead stars are pretty perfect together as two polar-opposite sisters. As Nicky struggles with an alcohol addiction and tries to get her life together, Chloe's quest for perfection drives a wedge between them. Banks and Biel are joined by performers like Kim Dickens, Matthew Modine, Gloria Reuben, Lorraine Toussaint, and Janel Moloney. Their names are sort of similar, but ultimately, both "The Good Daughter" and "The Better Sister" center on sisterhood ... and all its ups and downs.

#3502. After ‘Whalefall’ Flops, Can Imagine Entertainment Return to Box Office Glory with ‘How to Rob a Bank’?

“How to Rob a Bank” may benefit from doing just that. With career-low reviews for director David Leitch, the Amazon MGM Studios release has been tracking poorly and now looks unlikely to crack $10 million from 2,810 theaters in its domestic debut.

For the film’s production banner, Imagine Entertainment, it is shaping up to be a second theatrical non-starter after its high-concept survival thriller “Whalefall” — about a scuba diver trapped in the belly of a marine mammal — got beached after its October opening with just a $39 million total worldwide despite solid reviews. Neither “How to Rob a Bank” nor “Whalefall” marks an auspicious wide release homecoming for Imagine, even if Amazon and Disney, respectively, fronted the budget and marketing spend on the films. Related Stories ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: David Leitch’s Fun and Poppy YouTube Heist Movie Almost Gets Away with It Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money

The two features are Imagine’s first to play across more than 2,000 domestic screens in more than eight years; the last was Lionsgate’s buddy comedy “The Spy Who Dumped Me” in 2018. That’s practically an epoch for Imagine, which was founded by Ron Howard and Brian Grazer and spent its early years asserting itself as a theatrical force with hits like “Kindergarten Cop,” “Liar, Liar,” “The Nutty Professor,” and Howard’s own films, like “Apollo 13” and “How the Grinch Stole Christmas.” A spokesperson for the banner declined to comment for this report.

But Imagine, as with much of the industry, saw its focus on original, often adult-oriented programming hit diminishing returns in the past 20 years. The company’s biggest hit after 2010 was the 2016 Dan Brown adaptation “Inferno,” which, at $220 million global, earned less than half the gross that its 2009 predecessor “Angels & Demons” did.

Around that time, Imagine hitched its wagon to the then-burgeoning streaming industry, expanding its focus on television projects and aggressively branching into the documentary market, as theatrical features fell by the wayside. Packages for narrative features like “Tick, Tick… Boom!” and “The Beanie Bubble” were sold off to streaming services. But with an industrywide reawakening to the benefits of theatrical (which has even drawn in Netflix), along with a waning demand for unscripted programming, Imagine is now at the start of its return to wide-release, big-screen features.

There were some false starts along the way. Notably, Howard’s own 2022 rescue thriller “Thirteen Lives” had originally been set up at MGM before the studio’s acquisition by Amazon, which then executed an extremely limited theatrical release and opted out of reporting box office. The film’s star Viggo Mortensen later slammed the decision. Then there was Howard’s island-set thriller “Eden,” which sold to the mostly digital-focused distributor Vertical after debuting to withering reviews. And Luca Guadagnino’s post-#MeToo morality thriller “After the Hunt” never cracked 1,300 theaters from Amazon MGM after critics ripped it apart at Venice Film Festival. Many of these films carried hefty price tags — “Eden” had a $35 million net budget, while “After the Hunt” cost $80 million to produce.

“How to Rob a Bank,” co-produced by director Leitch’s 87North, faces a significant climb to any theatrical success with a $40 million production budget and intense Thanksgiving season competition incoming. Imagine has a more promising (though less novel) plan to lean further into IP in 2027. Another Amazon MGM release, the legacy sequel comedy “Spaceballs: The New One,” will come in April. And Universal is distributing a Snoop Dogg biopic, which Imagine developed along with the rapper’s own Death Row Pictures. Can Imagine find the same success with Snoop’s story that it did with “8 Mile”?

More original is the Adam Driver military thriller “Alone at Dawn,” directed by Howard himself, which shot in 2025 and is slated for a Christmas 2027 theatrical release from Amazon MGM. Further down the line, Imagine is developing a sequel to “How the Grinch Stole Christmas,” with Jim Carrey tapped to return. The first film was the top-grossing North American release of 2000 and remains a high watermark for Imagine’s commercial success.

Imagine Entertainment’s future of theatrical IP also comes after years of murmurs that the banner was fielding suitors amid its rise in the documentary space, including a Variety report of a 2021 valuation around $800 million and a 2022 report from TheWrap that a $700 million valuation deal with Centricus Asset Management Ltd. had fallen through. But more recently, TheWrap reported on October 1 that majority stakeholder The Raine Group, which came aboard for $100 million in 2016, was in talks to sell its 51 percent ownership to private equity; an Imagine representative issued an emphatic denial of the claim in the piece.

After a boom among independent production banners to start the decade, the business has faced growing instability over recent years, with shrinking valuations and sharp cutbacks in content spending. For decades, Imagine has been one of the industry leaders in the space, but “How to Rob a Bank” and “Whalefall” are the first test of whether it can reassert itself as a theatrical hitmaker. If the poor tracking for “Rob a Bank” pans out, it’ll then look to “Spaceballs” for, as the joke in Mel Brooks’ 1987 goes, “The Search for More Money.”

#3501. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.
