#3500. Daniel Craig's Most Disappointing Bond Film Quietly Exits Streaming This Month

Craig’s time as 007 may be over, but there’s still time to revisit one of his most explosive adventures

Daniel Craig's time as James Bond may be over, but his legacy as the iconic British spy is still being felt across Hollywood. After five films and 15 years in the role, Craig helped usher in a grittier era for the long-running franchise, delivering some of 007's most memorable big-screen adventures along the way.

Now, the search for his successor is heating up. No replacement has been officially announced, but fans could find out who will inherit the famous tuxedo before the end of the year. While audiences wait for the next chapter of the franchise, there's an opportunity to revisit one of Craig's Bond adventures — unfortunately, it's leaving streaming soon and time is running out to watch it again.

Released in 2008, Quantum of Solace picks up shortly after the events of Casino Royale, with James Bond still dealing with the death of Vesper Lynd, the woman he fell in love with during his previous mission.

Determined to uncover the truth behind her betrayal and death, Bond sets out to track down the people responsible. His investigation leads him to Dominic Greene, a ruthless businessman secretly working with a mysterious organization known as Quantum. Greene is plotting to seize control of a valuable natural resource, putting Bond on a collision course with a dangerous conspiracy.

Craig returns as 007, with Olga Kurylenko (Black Widow) joining the cast as Camille Montes, a woman with her own reasons for seeking revenge against Greene. Mathieu Amalric (The Grand Budapest Hotel) plays the film's main antagonist, while Judi Dench returns as M.

Quantum of Solace is an important entry in Craig's Bond era, but its critical reception was somewhat divided. The film currently holds a 63% critics score on Rotten Tomatoes, alongside a 58% audience score. Most reviews praised its intense action sequences and Craig's performance, although some felt it has a weaker story than Casino Royale.

Still, with plenty of explosive action and another compelling performance from Craig, Quantum of Solace is worth revisiting for anyone looking to celebrate his time as 007.

#3499. Stacy Keach Played A Villain In One Of The Best Batman Movies Of All Time

Actor Stacy Keach passed away on November 10, 2026, leaving behind a huge list of film, television, and theatre credits across his lifetime. Typecasting never really caught up with Keach. He could play diametrically different characters, like how he acted as both the morally upright Warden Henry Pope in "Prison Break" and Neo-Nazi leader Cameron Alexander in "American History X."

Even so, Keach's deep voice often coded him as a tough guy you don't want to mess with. DC Comics and Batman fans will recognize that voice from "Batman: Mask of the Phantasm," one of the best Batman movies, animated or otherwise. The titular villain is a skull-masked, scythe-wielding vigilante targeting gangsters in Gotham City. Unlike Batman (Kevin Conroy), the Phantasm employs lethal force.

Keach voices the Phantasm (at least when they're wearing their mask). The Phantasm doesn't say that much, admittedly, because silence serves their menacing presence more. But whenever the Phantasm first appears in a plume of smoke, they announce themselves with this line: "[Name], your angel of death awaits!" Keach makes the Phantasm's voice live up to those words. It's deep and ghostly, with an echo that sounds like he is genuinely an apparition from beyond the mortal plane.

"Mask of the Phantasm" features a dual timeline structure; half of the movie takes place in Bruce Wayne's youth before he becomes Batman. He romances Andrea Beaumont (Dana Delany), the woman he almost chose over becoming Batman. Keach has a second role in this storyline as Carl Beaumont, Andrea's financier father. Naturally, you then make the leap (subconsciously or not) in thinking that Carl is the Phantasm, especially once we learn he was once indebted to the gangsters the Phantasm is killing in the present. That's just what the movie wants you to think.

Okay, enough hiding behind spoilers: The Phantasm is actually Andrea herself. She and her father had to flee the country to dodge his loan shark debtors, which is why she canceled her engagement to Bruce all those years ago. But the gangsters caught up to the Beaumonts, killed Carl, and now Andrea is back for revenge. (Amusingly, the twist of Andrea being the Phantasm was spoiled by some tie-in toys.)

Keach's part as Carl gets back to his acting range. He plays, essentially, the Grim Reaper and a terrified father, and he's great in both parts. The red herring of Carl being the Phantasm becomes text late in the movie, after Andrea and Bruce rekindle their relationship and she explains why she left him — except for the part that her dad is dead. Diegetically, Andrea has given her alter ego her father's voice to throw suspicion off herself. While framing her father might dishonor his memory, she's also playing the part of Carl Beaumont's vengeful spirit to kill his killers.

Batman having a romantic connection with a foe is nothing new — just ask Catwoman or Talia al Ghul. The Phantasm's backstory has the foundation for a redemption, but happy endings are hard to come by in Gotham City. "Mask of the Phantasm" commits to being a romantic tragedy; Batman doesn't reach or redeem Andrea, who chooses her vengeance. The final two scenes of the film show Andrea and then Bruce, both alone again. But at least Batman still has Gotham.

"Mask of the Phantasm" remains widely beloved and is often considered the late Kevin Conroy's greatest performance as Batman. Stacy Keach as the Phantasm was an essential ingredient, too, and may he also rest in peace.

Bose has issued a recall of more than 670,000 lithium-ion battery packs used in the company's S1 Pro and S1 Pro+ Bluetooth speaker systems due to overheating issues.

According to a Consumer Product Safety Commission announcement, Bose has received reports of the battery packs overheating to the point of melting, producing smoke or catching fire. Fortunately, no injuries have been reported.

The recall specifically affects battery packs that include any one of the following six digits in the serial numbers: 083723, 078352, 084105, 078591, 078592, 084106, or 086409. You can find the 17-digit number on the label printed on the bottom of the pack.

These packs were sold both with the S1 Pro and S1 Pro+ speakers as well as accessories, for between $100 and $160 from December 2017 through July 2026. The speaker systems cost $700.

In total, 634,759 were sold in the US, with an additional 35,400 in Canada.

If you have the S1 Pro or S1 Pro+ Portable Bluetooth Speaker Systems, Bose requests that you stop using the battery packs immediately and remove them from the speakers. You can still use the speakers connected to AC power.

If you have an uninstalled battery pack, you just need to find the serial number and send it to Bose.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Bose is asking owners to register and provide the serial number at http://www.bose.com/support/s1-battery-recall. The company is providing a free replacement battery pack.

You'll need to dispose of the battery safely, which means do not just throw the battery pack in the trash or in used battery recycling boxes at retail or home improvement stores. Lithium-ion batteries must be disposed of differently from other batteries because of the greater risk of fire.

You'll need to look up your local municipality's household hazardous waste collection center. You should contact the center because not everyone accepts lithium-ion batteries. They will generally be able to point you in the right direction.

#3497. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

#3496. ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Is Absolutely Insufferable in a Dull and Dreary Christmas Carol

A Sauvage and jowly overactor in dire need of career rehabilitation could hardly ask for a better part to play than Ebenezer Scrooge. He’s a cruel miser of a man who comes to learn the error of his ways over the course of a ghost story that preys upon Christian precepts of redemption and forgiveness (along with the more secular warm and fuzzies of seeing a bad guy discover the joys of being good). Indeed, what is “cancel culture” if not a shackled delusion that visits self-made pariahs in the dead of night, and what is Charles Dickens’ “A Christmas Carol” if not a plea to believe that even the most odious of souls are still capable of being saved? Related Stories Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

It’s been reported that Johnny Depp accepted the title role of Ti West’s “Ebenezer” at a fraction of his usual rate, but I suspect that he probably would have done this movie for free. While the embattled star earned more than $250 million for his work on the “Pirates of the Caribbean” franchise, even that psychotic number pales in comparison to the pricelessness of starring in a major studio Christmas movie that allows him to look just left of the camera and say lines like “I’m not the man I was!” and “I was once good, and I know I can be again!” before his character saves a cherubic little boy from certain death and invites a freezing beggar inside for a warm cup of tea. If an old crank like Scrooge can make his way back toward grace, why not the convicted star of “Mortdecai,” and the alleged perpetrator of several even more serious crimes?

Johnny Depp may prefer for that to be framed as a rhetorical question, but his insufferable turn as literature’s most cantankerous moneylender demands an honest answer. For me, that answer is rather straightforward: While Depp has never been the subtlest of actors, his post-Sparrow pivot away from artistic curiosity has distended his talents into such a grotesque caricature of their former charm that “Ebenezer” left me feeling like I may never be able to empathize with his screen presence again.

Scrooge is obviously a scenery-chewer’s dream, but the crescent arc he traces from grinch to Christmas miracle is only believable enough to sustain Dickens’ fable if you believe it on both ends. Depp’s performance — an advent calendar of empty affectations without a soul to anchor them, every shot full of face and bereft of feeling — makes that exceedingly difficult. His offscreen unsavoriness certainly doesn’t help, but there’s a more immediate problem when the lights go down, one that makes him a unique case among Hollywood’s tainted array of mega-star actors: He seems to have become very bad at acting. Whatever my feelings about Depp as a human being, the truth is that I didn’t buy him as a glowering monster any more than I bought him as a beaming man who’s grown “better than his word.”

An unengaging Ebenezer is a tough break for a movie called “Ebenezer,” and screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern’s fidelity to the source material doesn’t exactly leave West with a wealth of opportunities to compensate for such fatal miscasting. West’s take on the holiday classic is faithful to the core — no Muppets, no ghosts of girlfriends past, no uncanny mo-capped Jim Carrey. As you might expect from the director of indie genre standouts like “Pearl” and “The House of the Devil,” West’s big idea is to scare the Dickens out of us by turning up the volume on this story’s implicit scariness. Sometimes literally, as this PG-13 carol offers a small handful of gentle jump-scares.

“Ebenezer” isn’t a horror movie in the strictest sense, but West does what he can to play up the fear that eventually terrifies Scrooge into giving a shit about his fellow man. Most — or all — of those flourishes are purely cosmetic in nature, and hellbent on sucking every glimmer of life out of Victorian England. Scrooge’s office has never looked more haunted, as Checco Varese’s grimdark cinematography and Eve Stewart’s Yharnam-esque production design combine to create a London that’s in dire need of Christmas cheer (the vibe should go a long way with tweenage audiences eager for a bit of spice with their holiday viewing, though I suspect the whole thing is too staid and oppressive to become any kind of perennial favorite).

And since West would sooner die than pass up a chance for death, this version of the story treats us to a musty prologue where we actually get to see Ebenezer’s business partner bite the dust with his mouth wide open (Marley is played by Ian McKellen in what currently stands as the most “remember ‘The Christophers?’” performance of the year). From there, the action skips forward to Christmas Eve 1843, whence Ebenezer is inflicting his usual “Bah, humbug!” routine on poor Bob Cratchit (Rupert Grint), the underpaid clerk he resents for taking the next day off (HR being a decidedly 20th-century invention). But the fates have plans of their own for the bitter-cold businessman, who promptly pisses himself when the ghost of old Marley bursts into his miserable bedchamber later that night.

Reaction shots ensue, as Depp curdles his face into a series of the most exaggerated expressions since the death of silent cinema, every one of them betraying his character’s frigidness. This Ebenezer takes an active pleasure in being cruel, which not only makes him more detestable (which is fine), but also endows him with an innate capacity for joy that makes the rest of the movie feel like it’s walking in circles (which is less fine). Given that Depp’s performance is only as wide as his lips and as deep as his pockets, it seems wasteful that we should have to walk through the hollows of Ebenezer’s past, present, and future in order to fix him — it would be easier and equally meaningful to just push the corners of his mouth into a smile.

Of course, that would deprive us of the “holy shit, that’s Andrea Riseborough” fun of the “To Leslie” star’s Ghost of Christmas Past, a white-eyed ghoul who looks like a spirit from “The Conjuring” who popped up for a sudden jolt and then forgot to leave the frame. She’s the most amusing part of a familiar tour through the sadness of Ebenezer’s childhood, where he was bullied by the other kids and kept apart from his beloved older sister. Tramell Tillman is equally compelling as the boisterous Ghost of Christmas Present, though his bizarre character design — a round-bellied man whose face appears to be rotting to pieces in real-time — turns out to be reverse-engineered from an unnerving reveal that both honors Dickens’ text and also underlines West’s limited conviction to rejuvenate it with the visceral immediacy of a horror film (his commitment to the bit falls well short of the Robert Eggers-level follow-through that conceit demands).

Given the emphasis the director puts on the film’s genre spin, it’s ironic and surprising that “Ebenezer” is at its best when it focuses on the most basic human elements of its story, if only because the supporting characters offer such a welcome contrast to whatever Depp is doing. Sam Claflin and Daisy Ridley don’t have a whole lot to do as Ebenezer’s kind-hearted nephew Fred and his wife Clara (respectively), but the film takes pains to stress how sad it is that Scrooge is Fred’s last connection to his dead mother, and it’s touching to see how much it would mean for him to have a cordial relationship with the old miser.

It is considerably less touching to see Ebenezer arrive at a mutual feeling after palling around with the film’s Nazgûl-coded Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come (Robert Strange, cloaked in CGI), who forces the misanthrope to face the emptiness of his own miserable existence. “The flame of humanity still flickers within you,” someone tells Scrooge, but the slapstick pageantry of Depp’s performance sabotages the movie by keeping that flame at a low simmer from the start. I didn’t believe the fire had ever gone out any more than I believed that it was eventually rekindled, as this Ebenezer Scrooge is far too elastic and self-amused to convincingly suggest that he’s experiencing a permanent change of heart. He can’t even sustain a facial expression for more than a few seconds before he starts mugging around in search of another one.

There will, of course, be those who insist that I only panned “Ebenezer” because Johnny Depp is in it, and I suppose they’re at least half-right about that, if not quite for the reason they assume. The truth is that it would be a lot more interesting and true to the spirit of Dickens’ classic if I liked this movie in spite of Depp rather than disliking it because of him, as I can’t help but share the author’s opinion that everyone is theoretically capable of redemption, be it measure by measure or miraculously complete.

Alas, the actor’s “comeback” performance is just yet another thing that he ought to be sorry for.

Paramount Pictures will release “Ebenezer” in theaters on Friday, November 13.

#3495. 'Avatar: Seven Havens’ Season 2 Release Date Announcement Includes Some Shocking Good News

Book 2: Discovery will feature a big reunion and more answers about Korra

Book 2: Discovery will feature a big reunion and more answers about Korra

Avatar: Seven Havens spent its entire first season in the Haven of Ellora, but as the show's title makes clear, that's just one of many Havens spread across this post-apocalyptic landscape. After a huge concentration of that energy exploded near Ellora, it created a large dome that threatened to consume the entire Haven. Only by unblocking her own root chakra was Pavi able to redirect the energy through her body and into the sky, where it manifested as an aurora. Based on a vision she received right after, another Haven called the Floating Isles needs her help. So at the end of Book 1, Pavi sets out into the Harshlands with Jae (Major Curda) at her side.

While inside the Anomaly dome, however, Pavi had learned the truth about her and Nisha’s past: Their parents had tried to surrender Nisha to the White Lotus, fearing her powers. In a fit of despair, Nisha emitted a jolt of red lightning that caused a rockside to seemingly crush her parents and sever Pavi’s leg. The twins then have a fight, and Pavi decides to leave Nisha behind. That accounts for the aforementioned “unresolved issues.”

My best guess about the “mysterious spirit energy Pavi released” has a lot to do with the state of the world. Bender birth rates are on the decline, spirits are virtually nonexistent, and the land itself is in a sorry state of decay. It would appear that spiritual energy worldwide has ceased flowing properly. Which is why the series has put so much emphasis on chakras. If the flow of energy in the world has stagnated into gross pockets of stale liquid like the red pool seen underneath Ellora, then transforming it back into its natural state could be precisely the mission that the Avatar(s) must accomplish to fix the world.

Pavi learning more about what happened to Korra in Book 2 is a welcome detail that feels like a must. One of Book 1’s more compelling sub-plots involves a flashback that the twins experience of Korra seemingly destroying Republic City. Everybody blames her for the Cataclysm, but there must be a deeper explanation there. What really happened to Avatar Korra?

The official description for Book 2 confirms, like I theorized, that the next stop on the Avatar’s journey after the Floating Isles is New Ba Sing Se. Pavi’s visions draw a clear connection between saving the Seven Havens and unblocking her own seven chakras. Ellora is the red earth chakra associated with survival and blocked by fear. Since the Floating Isles is associated with the color orange, we know it’s the second chakra which focuses on pleasure and is blocked by guilt.

In the Seven Havens world map shown during the show’s opening credits, the Haven associated with the yellow chakra is located in the northeast corner of what used to be the Earth Kingdom, which is exactly where Ba Sing Se was located until the Cataclysm. The third chakra is associated with willpower and is blocked by shame. That makes New Ba Sing Se a fitting place for the twins to reunite and grapple with “all their unresolved issues.” Think of the shame Nisha feels for what she did to their family. Think of the shame Pavi probably feels for abandoning Nisha after everything they’ve both gone through. And think of the shame they both feel for being the dual reincarnation of Avatar Korra, the person everyone thinks destroyed the world.

Letting go of all this shame seems like a natural place for Book 2 to go, which also means we’re probably going to get some cleaner answers about what actually caused the Cataclysm and what Korra’s real role was in it all.

To hear that Nisha has a parallel role that intersects with her sister again in Book 2 is a relief. Plenty of fans have voiced concerns about Seven Havens becoming “the Pavi show.” The finale positioned Pavi as the Avatar setting out to fix the world, while Nisha simply stayed behind and was praised as the hero of Ellora. For them to reunite seems like a wise decision.

Book 1 also established a practical reason for Nisha to travel. When members of the White Lotus tested her bending powers, they said that she needed to train in other Havens to sharpen her skills. And when Nisha exposed herself as the Avatar to fight Agam (Sakina Jaffrey) during the summit, Agam made a point to say that Nisha only knows Elloran bending styles. Each Haven seemingly has its own bending techniques, which could position New Ba Sing Se as a training destination that puts her on a collision course with Pavi, rather than somewhere she visits specifically to find her sister. Although, whatever information Nisha uncovers about the energy Pavi released could be so important that she has to find Pavi to tell her.

Paramount Plus hasn’t announced a premiere date or title for Book 3, but the streamer did confirm that it will also consist of 13 episodes and be released later in 2027. Book 4 will conclude the series, with release details still to come.

The accelerated release schedule means we may see substantially more of this world before the end of next year. If Book 2 covers the Floating Isles and New Ba Sing Se, four Havens remain for the final two seasons.

Following the chakra sequence, the next two would be green and blue: the heart chakra, which deals with love and is blocked by grief, and the sound chakra, which deals with truth and is blocked by lies. Feather Mountain and Akasha are possible matches, though their respective colors remain unconfirmed. Beyond those lie the light chakra, concerned with insight and blocked by illusion, and the final thought or crown chakra, associated with cosmic energy and blocked by earthly attachment. The light chakra appears to be located in or near the ruins of the old Fire Nation, and Republic Forest is almost certainly the final stop.

That gives the remaining story a framework, but it doesn’t dictate who visits each location or when. The twins could continue together after New Ba Sing Se or go their separate ways to help the remaining Havens separately. Saving Ellora felt like a big deal that took an entire season, but we’re about to step into a much bigger world in May when Book 2 begins.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3494. No, We Aren’t All Eating 'Too Much' Protein

If you’ll permit me a rant—I promise to make it fact-filled and interesting—I am sick of the articles that seem to pop up every few months claiming that we are all eating “too much” protein. They convey an inaccurate picture of how the body uses protein, and they demonize perfectly healthy meals that happen to be high in protein. It’s time to set the record straight.

It is true that most of us eat more than the RDA (recommended daily allowance) of protein, but that's a good thing—the RDA is meant as a minimum. It's true that protein-boosted foods are trendy, and that they're not necessarily great dietary choices in the big picture. It's also true that you can eat a healthy diet with little to no meat, but meat is not synonymous with protein. Let's look at what we actually know about the role of protein in a healthy diet, and how to tell if you're eating too much or too little.

As a refresher, protein is one of the three calorie-containing macronutrients (fats, carbs, protein) that make up most of the food we eat. Proteins are made of amino acids, and these amino acids are required for the growth, repair, and functioning of our bodies.

We can get protein from a variety of sources. Meats are particularly protein-dense; a chicken breast contains about 35 grams of protein. Other animal products, like milk and eggs, are also rich in protein. Plant-based foods tend to have less protein than animal products, but it’s not hard to meet or exceed protein requirements even on a vegan diet. Beans, grains, and soy products like tofu contain significant amounts of protein, for example.

If you’d like a cheat sheet on how much protein you’re supposed to eat based on your activity level, you can find one here. And that’s a good place to start dissecting this “too much protein” myth, because before we can declare an amount of protein to be “too much,” we need to understand how much is “enough.”

The government communicates targets for different nutrients to encourage us all to eat a healthy, balanced diet. These targets are the basis for the “% daily value” labels on the back of packaged foods, and for the nutrient makeup of school lunches. The RDA, or recommended daily allowance, is defined as “the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all (97 to 98 percent) healthy individuals in a group.”

In other words, if 100% of us were to eat the RDA of protein, at least 97% of us would be getting enough protein—we'd be meeting the minimum to be healthy. That's right, this number is a minimum to avoid malnutrition, not a maximum, and not a recommendation for optimal health.

By the way, if you're wondering how that number is determined? For protein, it is based on nitrogen balance. Humans break down proteins, as part of our body’s daily function, and we excrete nitrogen as a result. If you eat enough protein (which contains nitrogen), the amount of nitrogen you excrete will be the same as, or more than, the amount you eat. In other words, if you aren’t breaking your own body proteins down (in excess of what you eat), then whatever you’re eating must be, in some sense, enough.

In this way of thinking, the RDA is the minimum to stay healthy. More is fine; less would mean that you may not be getting enough. For some nutrients, there is also an UL, or upper limit, telling you that more than a certain amount is too much. Upper limits are calculated for vitamins and minerals; there is no upper limit defined for protein.

Therefore, there is no official definition for “too much” protein. If somebody eats more than the RDA, they’re not eating too much; they’re just eating more than the minimum. You’re supposed to eat more than the minimum.

The RDA for protein is set at 46 grams per day for a 125-pound woman, and at 56 grams per day for a 154-pound man. (The USDA chose those as their examples.) That’s based on an RDA of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram bodyweight, which works out to 0.36 grams per pound. So a 200-pound person would need 72 grams of protein per day.

This USDA report found that most adult men average roughly 90 to 100 grams of protein per day, although men aged 70 and up only get about 80 grams of protein per day. Women tend to average around 70 grams per day, with those aged 70 and up averaging 62 grams.

Above the RDA? Yes. Too much? I don’t see any way of arguing that. And before you say that we’re getting almost double the recommendation, let's check the math. Those RDA numbers are for 125- and 154-pound people. On the other hand, the averages for what we eat are based on actual people, not ideals. The average American man is 200 pounds, and the average American woman is 171 pounds. So, to compare the numbers:

The average woman is 171 pounds, so her RDA would be 62 grams per day. (Women, on average, eat 70 grams of protein per day.)

The average man is 200 pounds, so his RDA would be 72 grams per day. (Men, on average, eat 90 to 100 grams of protein per day.)

Again, there’s no need to stick to the minimum; going 8 grams over, or even 28 grams over, is fine. It’s probably better to go over than to just scrape by, and many of us arguably don’t get enough. Let me explain.

Let’s start with older adults. Not only does protein intake tend to decrease with age, older adults are vulnerable to issues that stem from a loss of muscle mass. People tend to lose 3-5% of their muscle mass per decade starting at age 30, but strength training and protein intake can support maintaining our muscle, and thus likely prevent or reduce that decline.

The Dietary Guidelines include a note that “About 50 percent of women and 30 percent of men 71 and older fall short of protein foods recommendations.” Meanwhile, a study found that older adults who don’t meet the recommendations are “more likely to be limited when stooping, crouching, or kneeling, standing or sitting for long periods, walking up 10 steps, preparing meals, and walking for a quarter mile.”

So even if it’s true that the average adult gets more protein than recommended, there are clearly a lot of elderly folks who don’t. These are the same people who have more issues functioning in everyday life. This may be a chicken-and-egg situation—was the functional decline a cause or an effect of the change in their diet?—but this sure does not seem to be a group of people who should be eating less protein.

There’s another large group of people who benefit from more, not less, protein: people who are pregnant or lactating. Instead of 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight (62 grams for a 171-pound person), the RDA for people who are pregnant or lactating is 0.5 grams/pound (so, 86 grams of protein per day).

When you’re pregnant, you also have higher caloric needs, so the increased total amount of food makes it easier to get the higher protein amount. Still, it makes more sense to spend your energy on making sure you’re getting enough protein, rather than worrying about getting too much.

You knew we were heading in this direction (I say between reps of barbell squats, wiping protein shake off my lips): People who exercise should get more protein than just the RDA.

While the fear-mongering “too much protein” articles sometimes mention that bodybuilders or elite athletes need their protein, they tend to hand-wave this away as a special concern that doesn’t apply to normal people. But I think it’s worth a closer look—and honestly, this situation applies to a lot more people than just a few athletes.

Officially, there isn’t an RDA for athletes; people who exercise can stave off malnutrition with the same 0.36 grams per pound as everyone else. But that doesn’t mean that the RDA is the best target to aim for.

The International Association of Athletics Federations, which governs track and field competitions, recommends that most athletes who are maintaining or gaining weight eat 0.59 to 0.77 grams of protein per pound of bodyweight per day. That’s 101 to 131 grams for the average 171-pound woman, and 118 to 154 grams for a 200-pound man.

A group of organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, largely agrees, recommending a range from 0.54 to 0.9 grams per pound for all athletes whose weight is stable or gaining. That includes people who do endurance training like distance running, as well as strength athletes whose exercise involves mainly lifting weights. Those ranges would go as high as 153 grams for our 171-pound woman, and 180 grams for our 200-pound man.

You don’t need to be an Olympian to consider yourself an “athlete” in this sense. If you’re training for a half marathon, you’re doing plenty of distance running, and should fuel accordingly. And if you’re “just” lifting weights in the gym, but taking it seriously enough that you’re training regularly and working hard, you should consider eating in these ranges as well.

Dieting to lose weight is not only a popular American pastime, it’s also arguably good for at least some people's health. If you’ve been on a diet recently, or if you’re planning to go on one, you aren’t a person who should settle for the RDA either.

Research shows that protein intake (and strength training—they go together!) is important to maintain muscle mass when we’re losing weight. After all, you’re aiming for fat loss, not trying to get your muscles to waste away. Muscle loss is especially a concern with weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, but any dieter should be aware of this issue.

For example, this study found that diets ranging from 0.48 to 0.72 grams of protein per kg of body weight (that’s 82 to 123 grams for our 171-pound woman, 96 to 144 for our 200-pound man) resulted in less weight regain after the diet, and helped people to maintain muscle mass and feel more full while they were dieting.

And if you’re losing weight and exercising? The IAAF recommends that athletes who are “undertaking high-quality weight loss” need at least 0.72 grams per pound of bodyweight, and possibly as much as 1.09 grams per pound. That would be 186 grams for a 171-pound athlete, or 218 grams for a 200-pound athlete. Most people won’t need to go that high, and it’s unclear whether athletes need to go that high. But I’m including these numbers so you see how high the ranges actually go.

Ultimately, weight loss is widely understood to be more effective and have healthier results with higher protein intakes rather than lower ones. When people focus on just eating less, without thinking about what their diet actually consists of, it’s easy to forget about protein. But the evidence suggests that you should increase protein when you’re decreasing overall calories.

The idea that protein causes weight gain is a common talking point in those articles about “too much” protein, and it’s sort of true—but it also doesn’t mean what you think it means.

When you eat more food than your body needs, your body can store it as fat. That’s true no matter what the excess is made of—protein, carbs, fat, or even alcohol. The protein you eat gets used for many different things in your body. You can build it into muscle tissue, use it for growth and repair of different kinds of cells, and so on. You can also use it for energy—basically, burning it for the calories.

So if you were eating a perfectly balanced diet, and then decided to add an extra 100 grams of protein per day, then sure, a lot of that protein would be used for energy, and since we’d have excess energy, it would get stored as fat.

But if you ate more protein, but that protein replaced other foods in your diet, then there would be no excess calories to store. Nobody is saying you should chug a couple of protein shakes on top of your regular diet. They’re saying (I’m saying) that you should plan your meals and snacks to include more protein.

For example, if your regular lunch is a turkey-and-cheese sandwich with a side of chips, you could improve the protein content of your diet by adding more turkey to the sandwich and replacing the chips with an apple. Same total calories, but more protein. As long as your total calories for the day aren’t in excess of your needs, the “extra” protein won’t get stored as fat.

In general, high protein diets don’t have any serious health consequences. There’s a major exception, though: in some medical conditions, you may be told to limit your protein intake to protect your health.

For example, people with chronic kidney disease are often advised to use the RDA (0.36 grams per pound of body weight) as a maximum rather than a minimum. Your kidneys play a role in processing protein for excretion, so a lowered protein intake reduces the amount of work that a damaged kidney has to do. That said, once a person with chronic kidney disease begins dialysis, they may be advised to increase their protein intake for better health now that their body has help to handle the higher levels.

People with certain other disorders, like phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, may also be advised to eat a low-protein diet. Obviously, if you have one of these conditions, you should be getting your dietary advice from your medical team (ask for a referral to a dietitian!) rather than from general articles on the internet.

Besides those known medical issues, the occasional findings about eating “too much” protein tend to fit into the “X is good for you/X is bad for you” ricochet news cycle. They’re not holistic assessments of protein in general on health in general, but rather specific research questions that are still being figured out.

For example, this 2017 study found that a high-protein (and high-fiber) diet seemed to slightly worsen one measure of insulin resistance, but it also improved metabolic health and body composition. The researchers concluded that the subjects’ body chemistry was probably just responding appropriately to the changed nutrient content of their diet. A few years later, a study of high-BMI women with insulin resistance saw improvements to their insulin resistance on a high-protein diet.

Or to take another example, a study in 2024 found a link between high-protein diets and atherosclerosis. But if you look at what the researchers were actually studying, they were looking at how leucine (one amino acid found in protein) affects the mTOR biochemical pathway in certain types of white blood cells. By the way, that mTOR pathway is involved in a lot more body processes than atherosclerosis, and does a lot of good things too.

So are these results interesting, and worth further study? Definitely. Worth changing protein recommendations? Only if this effect turns out (1) to actually lead to worse health outcomes, and (2) to outweigh the known benefits of higher protein. The body of evidence doesn’t yet support lowering protein recommendations, nor adding an upper limit.

So if protein is good for us, and most of us can’t really get “too much,” why are so many people arguing that we’re overdoing it? I think part of the reason is just misunderstanding (the writers don’t tend to have a background in nutrition and especially not in sports nutrition), but more often, I think they’re talking about a different issue entirely.

Often the “too much protein” stuff is just a way of talking about the environmental effects of meat consumption or dairy farming. People making this argument are trying to pry the double cheeseburgers out of our hands and reassure us that we’ll be okay. I don’t think an attack on protein is an appropriate way to make that point, since plant-based proteins exist and are a fine alternative. But I understand where they’re coming from.

Ultimately, if you’re trying to make the argument that we’re eating “too much” protein for our health, you really can’t do that without some evidence that we’re eating so much protein that it’s harming our health on a widespread level. And that evidence just doesn’t exist.

#3493. What Makes a Good Oscar Campaign? Just Ask Sony Classics’ Michael Barker and Tom Bernard

Sony Pictures Classics co-presidents Michael Barker and Tom Bernard have been the white whale of IndieWire’s “Screen Talk” podcast for years. Finally, they joined us for an engaging chat about the specialty label’s robust slate of films this year — and about Oscar campaigning and developments in the business.

Together, Barker and Bernard have reigned over the theatrical specialty universe for decades, believing in the theatrical model all along. And it seems to be roaring back, with a three-hour documentary at number two at the box office, and a foreign-language “Godzilla” movie at number one. Black Bear’s indie “Wicker” is in the top 10 and, earlier this fall, Sony Pictures Classics’ Sundance indie “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” starring Oscar hopeful John Turturro, was in the top 10. Related Stories ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Is Absolutely Insufferable in a Dull and Dreary Christmas Carol Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before

In this week’s podcast, Barker and Bernard talk about films including Pedro Almodóvar’s “Bitter Christmas”; Florian Zeller’s critically divisive but audience-appreciated “Bunker”; and the UK’s international Oscar entry from Iran, “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” which is also vying for Best Documentary Feature. They’re also backing the animated “Iron Boy” this year, plus Sundance winner “Bedford Park” and BAFTA winner “I Swear.” They also tease “Violette,” their latest acquisition, and the new film from “Amélie” director Jean-Pierre Jeunet.

Elsewhere on the podcast, we also mourn the unexpected passing of Chilean filmmaker Sebastian Lélio, dissect Letterboxd’s sales to The New York Times, and the dismissal of James Gunn and Peter Safran from DC Studios.

Plus, co-hosts Anne Thompson and Ryan Lattanzio strongly encourage audiences to see Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson’s excellent indie “Mouse” as it expands nationwide this weekend. Sophie Okonedo is hugely deserving of best supporting actress accolades, but the film needs critics to continue advocating for it.

#3492. Red X's True Identity In DC Comics Explained

DC Comics finally revealed the identity of one of its most mysterious Teen Titans villains in Teen Titans Academy #12, unmasking the student known as Red X as Brick Pettirosso. However, readers expecting the shocking reveal to put an end to the character's long-running mystery were in for another surprise. Almost immediately after Brick reveals himself, a second Red X appears, exposes the mastermind behind the entire scheme, and leaves Nightwing with an entirely new reason to worry.

The revelation answers one question while preserving another mystery that has followed Red X since his introduction in the original Teen Titans animated series. Although Dick Grayson originally created the disguise for an undercover mission, the identity of the impostor who eventually stole it was never revealed. DC's comics introduced their own take on the mystery through Future State: Teen Titans and Teen Titans Academy, but even after Brick's unmasking and subsequent murder, the true identity of the second Red X remains unknown.

Long before Red X appeared in DC's mainstream comic-book continuity, the masked character became one of the most intriguing mysteries in Cartoon Network's Teen Titans animated series. Originally, the identity was created by Dick Grayson, who used the disguise to infiltrate Slade's operation without compromising his identity as Robin. Once his undercover mission was exposed, Dick abandoned the costume, seemingly putting an end to the short-lived identity.

That changed when another individual appeared wearing the same Red X costume, immediately establishing himself as a dangerous rival for Robin. The second Red X possessed comparable fighting skills and acrobatic abilities, along with an impressive collection of gadgets and technology. His utility belt allowed him to teleport, turn invisible, and seemingly produce weapons whenever he needed them, making him a particularly difficult opponent for the Titans to apprehend. Despite several encounters with Robin, however, the animated series never revealed who was hiding behind the mask.

Jason Todd remains one of the most popular theories about the second Red X's identity. As Dick Grayson's successor as Robin, Todd would have had a similar background, training, and familiarity with the Boy Wonder. However, this has never been confirmed by DC. In fact, the publisher revisited the mystery in an April 2024 article on its official website, discussing several popular theories, including the possibility that Red X was a clone of Dick Grayson. Ultimately, the animated series never provided a definitive answer, leaving one of its most memorable mysteries intact.

Red X eventually made the jump from animation to DC's mainstream comic-book continuity through the publisher's Future State event in 2021. Among the many possible futures explored during the event was a particularly bleak version of the Teen Titans' history, in which Titans Tower had become a monument to the young heroes who died defending the world. Nightwing, Starfire, Beast Boy, Cyborg, and Raven were among the surviving members attempting to understand what happened and prevent the tragedy from becoming permanent.

The newest Teen Titans roster gets a mentor and leader who understands exactly what the team needs because he’s been where they are.

In Future State: Teen Titans #1, the surviving heroes turn to Red X, a mysterious former Titans Academy student, for help. Although his motives are initially questionable, he eventually joins the team in its fight against the catastrophic threat unleashed by one of the Academy's students. The story continues in the second issue, with Red X fighting alongside Nightwing, Raven, and the remaining heroes against the Four Riders of the Apocalypse. Rather than being an enemy of Raven, Red X is part of the group trying to save their world.The character's appearance was particularly interesting because DC was simultaneously exploring his origins in the ongoing Teen Titans Academy series. The comic followed the school's new generation of young heroes while gradually introducing another individual using the Red X identity. Readers were left wondering which student was behind the mask, with the story planting clues throughout its run. Eventually, the mystery reached its conclusion in Teen Titans Academy #12, although the answer was far more complicated than anyone expected.

The Academy's final confrontation reaches its breaking point when Red X turns against the Titans, insisting that Nightwing and his fellow heroes are exploiting their students. After attempting to convince the young heroes that their teachers are manipulating them, Red X finally removes his mask, revealing himself as Brick Pettirosso, one of the Academy's students. Brick's electromagnetic pulse abilities had provided an important clue to his identity, making the reveal especially satisfying for readers who had been paying attention to the series.

However, Brick's identity comes with an even more disturbing explanation. He genuinely believes Nightwing is his biological father and claims that being abandoned by him motivated his actions. Brick's surname, Pettirosso, is an Italian word for robin, another indication of the connection he believed he shared with Dick Grayson. Unfortunately, the story quickly establishes that Brick's understanding of his own history is built on a lie, and his supposed father has no idea who he actually is.

The real tragedy is that Brick was manipulated into becoming Red X long before he ever entered Titans Academy. The older Red X had taken him in and convinced him that Nightwing was his father, while teaching him to see the Titans as hypocritical adults who used young heroes as disposable weapons. Brick consequently believed that betraying the Academy was justified, even though the entire operation was designed to serve someone else's revenge.

The idea that Nightwing had a long-lost son is quickly put to rest when the Titans explain that they conducted blood tests on every student before admitting them to the Academy. The results confirm that Brick has no biological connection to Dick Grayson, leaving the heroes wondering how he could have been manipulated so thoroughly. The answer arrives almost immediately when the second Red X appears through his teleportation technology, ready to reveal the truth behind his elaborate plan.

The mysterious villain explains that he took Brick in and deliberately fabricated the story about Nightwing being his father. He also convinced the young boy that the Titans were using their students as pawns in a never-ending war against crime, giving Brick a personal reason to despise the organization. After years of manipulation, Brick was sent to infiltrate Titans Academy and undermine it from within. His supposed mission to protect the students was never anything more than a convenient way to carry out Red X's revenge against Nightwing.

Unfortunately, Brick discovers the truth too late. With his usefulness to the older villain at an end, the second Red X murders him directly in front of Nightwing, turning the young student's unmasking into an even more tragic revelation. Before disappearing through teleportation, the villain promises Nightwing that their conflict isn't over and that the two will eventually have another confrontation. Red X also claims that Dick ruined his life during his time as Robin, providing a glimpse of the personal hatred driving his elaborate scheme.

Nearly five years have passed since the events of Teen Titans Academy #12, but Nightwing's promised rematch with Red X has yet to materialize. The issue was released on February 22, 2022, and the older villain has not received a follow-up storyline that reveals his real identity or explains the full extent of his grudge against Dick Grayson. For all the answers provided by Brick's unmasking, the central mystery surrounding the older Red X remains unresolved.

The series also leaves another interesting question unanswered. Brick is identified as the fourth person to use the Red X identity, meaning there was another wearer whose identity was never established. Consequently, the comic-book mystery is even more complicated than the original animated series, with multiple characters having worn the same mask and only some of their stories receiving any explanation. Neither the identity of the third Red X nor the real name of the older mastermind is revealed in the issue.

DC reveals the identity of the hero who will replace a famous hero and Justice League member, with a subtle twist on their original name.

Following Teen Titans Academy #12, DC began building toward its Dark Crisis event, which shifted the publisher's attention toward the Justice League's apparent demise and the Titans' growing responsibilities. After the event, the Titans stepped up to replace the Justice League as the DC Universe's leading superhero team, with Nightwing taking on a major leadership role. However, the Justice League eventually returned through DC's All In initiative and Justice League Unlimited #1 in November 2024. Despite all these developments, the Red X storyline has remained without the promised resolution.

The character's continued absence leaves readers with two separate mysteries to consider. The original Teen Titans animated series never identified the individual who stole Dick Grayson's Red X identity, while DC's comics have yet to explain the full history of the multiple characters who adopted the disguise. Brick Pettirosso's death provided one answer, but the villain responsible for manipulating him is still out there, and Nightwing has yet to get the rematch he was promised.

Teen Titans Academy is available from DC Comics.

#3490. Sony's Bringing Back Spider-Man $2.5 Billion Hit With New Footage

Sony's $2.5 billion superhero hit isn't done dominating movie theaters yet

As Marvel Studios' release of Avengers Endgame: Encore proves, blockbuster movies can still dominate the box office, even after a multibillion dollar run. Sony is planning a rerelease of Spider-Man: Brand New Day to bring web-head-heads back to movie theaters — and like Endgame: Encore, the studio is adding new footage of Spider-Man's latest flick as an incentive.

Thanks to AMC Theatres, we now know what that rerelease will be called: Spider-Man: (Brand New) Brand New Day.

According to the AMC Theatres listing, Spider-Man: (Brand New) Brand New Day will be seven minutes long, with a run time of 2 hours 32 minutes. It's unclear how much of that will be new or restored footage, but it will be longer than Brand New Day's original theatrical run.

Spider-Man: (Brand New) Brand New Day is expected to arrive in movie theaters on Dec. 4.

According to a previous report from Deadline, the new footage will include at least one cut cameo from Spider-Man: Brand New Day that connects to the larger Marvel Cinematic Universe.

Deadline reports that Sony's planned theatrical rerelease of Spider-Man: Brand New Day will feature extra footage that includes an appearance from Rosario Dawson's character Claire Temple, aka Night Nurse. Dawson played Temple in multiple Netflix Marvel shows: Daredevil, Jessica Jones, Luke Cage, Iron Fist, and The Defenders. The Night Nurse had her own Marvel comic series in the early '70s, in which she tended to the medical needs of New York City's vigilante crime fighters (though that version of the character was named Linda Carter).

Dawson has said in interviews that she filmed a scene that was cut from the theatrical release of Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Deadline's report implies Sony has more than just a Claire Temple cameo in its pocket, saying there will be "more surprises in the extra footage."

If accurate, this wouldn't be the first time Sony has rereleased one of its Tom Holland-starring Spider-Man movies in theaters. The studio released an extended cut of Spider-Man: Far From Home and a "More Fun Stuff Version" of Spider-Man: No Way Home, the latter of which featured deleted scenes.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day's rerelease will no doubt help goose the film's box office haul, which currently stands at $2.52 billion, according to Box Office Mojo. Brand New Day is the highest-grossing movie at the domestic box office to date, with $959 million after two months in theaters. It's also the third-highest-grossing movie worldwide, behind Avengers: Endgame and the original Avatar. It's unlikely the rerelease would put Brand New Day on top; it's still $419 million behind Avengers: Endgame.

#3489. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

#3488. Ebenezer Ending Explainer: How Johnny Depp’s Remake Rewrites The Original Climax

Warning: The following contains full spoilers for Ebenezer.

Johnny Depp takes on one of literature's most recognizable characters in Ebenezer, a new supernatural reimagining of Charles Dickens' beloved Christmas novella A Christmas Carol.

Directed by Ti West, the film follows the miserable and grouchy businessman Ebenezer Scrooge as three haunting spirits force him to confront his past, reconsider his present, and witness the bleak future awaiting him if he refuses to change his miserable ways. Although the story follows the familiar structure of Dickens' classic tale, its conclusion introduces some particularly interesting differences that give Scrooge's redemption a new dimension.

Rather than ending with Scrooge simply becoming a kinder employer and a more generous member of society, Ebenezer gives him a more active role in changing the lives of the people he has mistreated. These changes make the ending one of the most distinctive aspects of the new adaptation. While the movie retains the hopeful spirit of Dickens' original story, it reimagines what redemption actually means for its central character.

The ending of Ebenezer sees Ebenezer Scrooge abandon his humbug ways and begin making meaningful changes to the lives of the people around him. However, the film goes considerably further than Dickens' original Christmas Carol novella in showing exactly how he intends to make amends.

After awakening on Christmas morning, Scrooge sets out to repair some of the relationships he has neglected throughout his life. One of his first gestures involves purchasing a turkey and delivering it personally to his nephew Fred and Fred's wife, Clara. This is particularly meaningful because Scrooge has spent years rejecting Fred's invitations and refusing to participate in family celebrations. This also marks a notable change from Dickens’ novella as, in the source material, Scrooge gifts the Cratchit family, not Fred and Clara, a Christmas turkey.

His generosity also extends to Belle, his former fiancée, although their relationship cannot simply be restored. Having discovered that she has moved on and established a successful writing career, Scrooge purchases one of her novels from a local book shop and leaves an unsigned letter inside. In it, he congratulates her on her achievements and expresses happiness that she has managed to build the life she wanted.

However, the most significant development comes when Scrooge finally approaches Bob Cratchit. Instead of simply offering his employee a raise, Scrooge proposes a substantial change to their professional relationship. He promises Cratchit a significant pay increase, allowing him to afford medical treatment for his son, Tiny Tim, and then reveals that he intends to make him a business partner. Scrooge walks Cratchit outside and says he wishes to rename their shop “Scrooge and Cratchit.”

Scrooge’s newfound treatment of Cratchit is arguably the biggest departure from Dickens' story. In the original novella, Scrooge promises to raise Cratchit's salary and support his struggling family, but Ebenezer takes the gesture much further by offering him a share in the business itself. The sign outside the building will eventually read Scrooge and Cratchit, marking the beginning of an entirely different partnership.

It's a fitting conclusion for a character whose relationship with money has defined almost every aspect of his existence. Scrooge doesn't simply decide to give away some of his wealth. Instead, he recognizes that he has the power to give other people opportunities that he previously denied them.

The ending is also unique in that Scrooge does not meet or visit the Cratchit family. Instead, much of the emotional weight of the climax is allocated to Scrooge’s relationship with Fred, who he admits he has neglected as Fred reminds him of painful memories of his late sister. This pivots finds West’s film approach the emotionality of Dickens’ classic tale from a different perspective.

Scrooge's decision to make Bob Cratchit his business partner is particularly significant when considering the film's opening flashback involving Jacob Marley.

The movie establishes that Scrooge and Marley were business partners before the latter's death seven years earlier. Their relationship offers an insight into the ruthless commercial environment that helped shape Scrooge's attitude toward money and the people working beneath him.

During the flashback, Marley demonstrates very little compassion for his employees. He openly belittles Bob Cratchit, treating him with the same disregard that defines the business's approach to its workers and customers. Scrooge eventually finds Marley dead after hearing a crash from another room, and he is the only person who attends his former partner's burial.

The film later reveals the consequences of the life Marley led through his ghostly appearance. Bound by heavy chains, he is condemned to wander the earth because of the selfish, money-driven existence he pursued.

This history makes Scrooge's final decision to bring Cratchit into the business particularly important. Marley represents the kind of businessman Scrooge once was, someone who measured success through financial accumulation while showing little concern for the people whose labor helped create his wealth.

By offering Cratchit a partnership, Scrooge effectively reverses the relationship he once shared with Marley. Instead of treating his employee as someone beneath him, he gives him an opportunity to become an equal.

The decision also suggests that Scrooge's transformation involves more than simply feeling guilty about his past. He understands that changing his behavior means changing the way he conducts his business and treats the people who depend on him.

Another interesting difference between Ebenezer and Dickens' novella concerns how Scrooge approaches the Cratchit family after his transformation.

In the original story, Scrooge famously sends a large turkey to the Cratchit household on Christmas morning, beginning his efforts to improve their circumstances. Many adaptations also include a scene in which he visits the family or otherwise makes his generosity known to them.

However, Ebenezer takes a slightly different approach. Scrooge doesn't actually enter the Cratchit home or spend Christmas with the family. Instead, he briefly looks through their window and watches as Tiny Tim offers a blessing to everyone.

The moment is significant because it demonstrates that Scrooge has finally begun to appreciate the happiness and affection that exist within the family, despite their difficult financial circumstances.

Earlier in the film, the Ghost of Christmas Present had shown him the hardships facing Bob and his loved ones, particularly the medical problems affecting Tiny Tim. Scrooge had also been forced to recognize how his unwillingness to pay his employee fairly had contributed to their struggles.

Watching the family from outside their home gives Scrooge another opportunity to reflect on what he has learned. He can see that their happiness isn't dependent on wealth, but their circumstances could be considerably improved if someone with his resources were willing to help.

Scrooge's attempt to reconnect with Belle is another important part of the ending, specifically because it demonstrates that his redemption isn't necessarily about recovering everything one has lost.

During his encounter with the Ghost of Christmas Past, Scrooge revisits his relationship with his former fiancée. Belle genuinely loved him, but his growing obsession with accumulating wealth put an end to their once loving relationship. Eventually, she recognized that money had become more important to him than their future together and decided to leave him.

The painful memory of Belle forces Scrooge to confront the devastating cost of his callous decisions. His fixation on financial success didn't simply make him an unpleasant businessman. It also prevented him from building a meaningful life with someone who genuinely cared about him.

By the time Scrooge awakens on Christmas morning, he has discovered that Belle has moved on. She has established a successful writing career, married someone else, spends time volunteering at a local shelter, and has built a life for herself without him.

But instead of attempting to win her back, Scrooge purchases one of her published novels and leaves an unsigned letter inside. His message congratulates her on her accomplishments and expresses his happiness that she has achieved the things she wanted in life. It's a relatively understated moment, but an important one for understanding the nature of Scrooge's transformation.

In many redemption stories, the central character's newfound goodness is demonstrated through the restoration of relationships that were previously damaged. However, Ebenezer recognizes that some things cannot simply be repaired. Belle has moved forward, and Scrooge's responsibility is to acknowledge her happiness rather than expect her to return to him. His gesture suggests that he has finally learned to care about someone else's happiness without expecting anything in return.

Despite its changes, Ebenezer retains the optimistic conclusion that has made Dickens' original story so enduring.

In both versions, Scrooge awakens on Christmas morning with a renewed appreciation for life and a determination to become a better person. His transformation is profound as he begins putting his newfound outlook into practice by showing generosity toward the people around him.

However, the film places considerably more emphasis on the practical consequences of his redemption. Dickens' novella concludes with Scrooge becoming somewhat of a second father figure to Tiny Tim, improving Cratchit's circumstances, and establishing himself as someone who knows how to keep Christmas throughout the year. His generosity and kindness demonstrate that even someone who has spent a lifetime behaving selfishly can change.

Ebenezer preserves that central message but gives Scrooge a more substantial role in changing the structures that contributed to other people's suffering, rather than stepping in and intervening in people’s lives directly. His decision to make Cratchit a business partner holds value as it demonstrates that he is willing to share not just his money, but also his power and opportunities.

A modern reimaging of Charles Dickens' classic tale of Ebenezer Scrooge, a wealthy miser who learns empathy on an eventful eve after communing with the dead.

#3487. ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations

The Cinema Eye Honors have revealed nominations for the 20th annual awards ceremony. Leading the pack are Poh Si Teng’s “American Doctor” and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “You Can See Everything” with seven nominations each.

The A24 Elizabeth Holmes movie also made Cinema Eye Honors history as the first film to be nominated for Nonfiction Feature, Direction, Editing, Production, Cinematography, and Original Score — along with the Audience Choice Prize.

Other films that fared well in nominations for the ceremony honoring outstanding artistic achievement in nonfiction and documentary films and series, which is often a bellwether for the Best Documentary Feature Oscar race, are Sara Dosa’s “Time and Water,” which scored six nominations, and recent Neon acquisition “NAZA,” which earned five nominations. Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, directors of the latter film, won at the 2025 Cinema Eye Honors for their previous film “No Other Land,” which won the Oscar for Best Documentary Feature. Related Stories What Makes a Good Oscar Campaign? Just Ask Sony Classics’ Michael Barker and Tom Bernard ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Is Absolutely Insufferable in a Dull and Dreary Christmas Carol

For individual recognition, “American Doctor” filmmaker Poh Si Teng has the most nominations this year, with five. “You Can See Everything” directors Fielder and Oppenheim received four apiece. Meanwhile, documentarian Jimmy Chin, who earned three nominations for “Everest: The Other Side,” which he co-directed with Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, moves into third on the all-time nominations list with 14 total nods.

Among distributors, HBO, National Geographic and Netflix tied with the most nominations, with each receiving 12 nods across all categories. Neon followed with nine nominations, while A24 and Watermelon Pictures both had seven.

After a first round of voting that saw nonfiction fans worldwide cast tens of thousands of votes for their favorite films, the Audience Choice nominees were announced. The last eight winners of the Best Documentary Feature Oscar— “Mr. Nobody Against Putin,” “No Other Land,” “20 Days in Mariupol,” “Navalny,” “Summer of Soul,” “My Octopus Teacher,” “American Factory,” and “Free Solo”— were all first contenders for the Audience Choice Prize. Second-round voting to determine this year’s winner will take place in December.

In addition to the previously announced Unforgettables Honorees, Broadcast nominees, and the Shorts List, Cinema Eye announced that Steve James’ documentary masterpiece, “Hoop Dreams,” will receive this year’s Legacy Award, presented to a classic nonfiction film that continues to inspire today’s working filmmakers.

This season, Cinema Eye will return to the Times Center in New York City, the home of its second and third editions, for its 20th Awards Ceremony on Monday, January 11, 2027. Cinema Eye Week, which includes events and activities for Cinema Eye nominees and honorees, kicks off in New York on Friday, January 8.

Wednesday, December 2: Shorts List Screenings, DCTV, New York

Saturday, December 5: Shorts List Screenings, Vidiots, Los Angeles

Monday, December 14: Shorts Nominees Announced and Final Audience Choice Voting Opens

Friday, January 8, 2026: Cinema Eye Week/end begins in New York City

Monday, January 11, 2026: 20th Annual Cinema Eye Honors Awards Ceremony

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That said, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.
